title: Malik Nabers practices in full Wednesday, Harbaugh says, 'I think he's ready to go'
description: Nabers hasn't played for the Giants since Week 4 of last year.
fullText:
The New York Giants had their first official practice of the regular season on Wednesday, and wide receiver Malik Nabers was a full practice participant.

Nabers has been recovering from the torn ACL that ended his 2025 campaign after just 4 games.

After practice, head coach John Harbaugh spoke to the media about Nabers' availability. He said, "I think he's [Nabers] ready to go." Harbaugh showed some gamesmanship and was not ready to declare outright that Nabers would play, but added that he believed if the wide receiver feels good, he will play.

New York opens the regular season Sunday night against the Dallas Cowboys for "Sunday Night Football." Nabers will have two more practices this week before game statuses are due Friday afternoon.

Nabers is heading into the third season of his career. As a rookie in 2024, he finished fifth in Offensive Rookie of the Year voting after posting 1,204 yards with seven touchdowns.

There was a lot of hype around Nabers last season after the team drafted quarterback Jaxson Dart. Unfortunately, the Giants' top wide receiver tore his ACL in Week 4 against the Los Angeles Chargers.

Before the injury, Nabers had played in four games and had 271 yards and two touchdowns.

This year, a healthy Nabers is expected to lead the Giants' wide receiving corps. He should be Dart's top receiving threat if he is out there. Nabers will be joined by third-round pick Malachi Fields and veterans Darnell Mooney and Odell Beckham Jr.

Nabers will look to bounce back in a big way in his 2026 season debut. He gets a familiar foe in the Cowboys, whom he has faced three times in his career. So far, Nabers has tallied 351 yards and two touchdowns on 29 receptions against New York's division rival.

title: Tarik Skubal confirms embarrassing Tigers secret with Max Muncy
description: Dodgers left-hander Tarik Skubal confirmed an embarrassing story during his time with the Tigers to teammate Max Muncy.
fullText:
The Los Angeles Dodgers continue to look like one of baseball's strongest World Series contenders as the 2026 MLB regular season enters its final weeks. Entering Wednesday night's game against the Cincinnati Reds, the Dodgers are 88-57 and seeking their seventh straight victory.

MORE: Red Sox make Sonny Gray, Ranger Suarez change ahead of Royals weekend series

Only 1.5 games behind the Milwaukee Brewers for the best record in the National League, the Dodgers have also seen one of baseball's biggest midseason acquisitions quickly become a key piece in their pursuit of a third straight World Series title.

The Dodgers acquired reigning back-to-back American League Cy Young Award winner Tarik Skubal from the Detroit Tigers ahead of the trade deadline. Since he arrived in Los Angeles, Skubal has started seven games and owns a 2.93 ERA and 48 strikeouts over 43 innings in a Dodgers uniform.

While Skubal has settled into his new city, a recent conversation with his teammate Max Muncy revealed a rather embarrassing detail about his time in Detroit. Muncy appeared on the show Foul Territory and revealed that Skubal confirmed the Tigers' old team plane was unable to fly across the country without stopping to refuel.

While the Tigers have since acquired a new team plane that is able to make cross-country flights, the revelation is a fitting detail for a franchise that has endured a disappointing season. Detroit enters Wednesday at 66-79 and well outside the American League playoff picture.

For Skubal, the difference has likely been night and day. Going from a middle-of-the-pack payroll team like the Tigers to the famously deep-pocketed Dodgers, Skubal has gotten the opportunity to experience some of the biggest luxuries afforded to major league stars.

Notably, the Dodgers are the only team in baseball this season to use two separate planes for road trips. One for players, and the other for staff. The way the team sees it, two planes grant more comfort for players, allowing further rest and recovery for their most important assets.

The differences between Detroit and Los Angeles certainly extend beyond air travel, but Skubal's story offers an interesting example of how differently organizations across the sport operate.

title: 10 Shows Like 'The Shards' You Should Watch Next
description: More series about rich kids behaving badly.
fullText:
I'm a little worried about Ryan Murphy. He hasn't debuted a new show in literal weeks, and Hulu's The Shards is only his third new series this year). On the plus side, it's as batshit (complimentary) as you might expect given the prolific producer has teamed with controversial author Bret Easton Ellis (Less Than Zero, American Psycho) to adapt his 2023 book—part high school memoir and part serial-killer thriller. With the season (series?) finale dropping this week, here are 10 more series about rich kids behaving badly to stream next.

Four one-time best friends reunite in Rosewood High School a year after the disappearance of the leader of their little clique, all having received threatening messages from the mysterious "A," who knows everything they did last summer...and pretty much all the rest of the time. Shoplifting, parents having affairs, students hooking up with teachers—you name it, it's happening in town, and A knows it all. After the prime suspect turns up dead, the girls are caught in the killer's web while trying to keep their secrets hidden. If seven juicy seasons and three A's aren't enough for you, there are three spin-offs. Stream Pretty Little Liars on Hulu and HBO Max.

Murder and mystery among rather shockingly well-dressed high schoolers? Check. This one's based on a young adult novel from Karen M. McManus involving a group of five high schoolers who show up to detention, only to have one of them die of what at first appears to be an allergic reaction. But My Girl this is not: Seems Simon ran a blog that revealed everyone’s secrets, meaning that pretty much everyone had a motive for murder. It’s a solid, effectively twisty-turny mystery series that dovetails surprisingly well into its second season. Stream One of Us is Lying on Peacock.

This top-tier teen drama stars Ama Qamata as Puleng Khumalo, a teenage girl who’s lived her entire life in the shadow of a sister who was taken as a baby by human traffickers (Puleng’s parents still hold a birthday celebration for the sister each year). When invited to a party by popular Fikile Bhele (Khosi Ngema), a student at an elite school in Cape Town, Puleng can’t help noticing similarities to her missing sibling. Puleng transfers to the school to get to the bottom of things and uncovers plenty of juicy high school drama and family secrets along the way. The show is elevated by its unexpected dramatic heft and a multitude of queer characters and storylines. Stream Blood & Water on Netflix.

Just another drama about a seemingly dull teenage overachiever providing security for a criminal sex ring by night. OK, so this one’s pretty unique, blending dark comedy and action with hints of relationship drama and, you know, the Korean sex trade. Needing some extra money, Oh Ji-soo has this specific gig when he’s not in school, but is otherwise a typical teenage doofus. His friend Gyu-ri comes from a wealthy family, but still wants in when she learns about Ji-soo’s sideline. Before long, both competitors and the police begin to circle, and life for the teens gets considerably more complicated, violent, and dangerous. Stream Extracurricular on Netflix.

Juicy import Elite follows a group of working-class friends who earn scholarships to Las Encinas, a fictional private school that is, in the show’s universe, the most exclusive in Spain. What they find there is snobbery, mystery, murder, and lots and lots of sex (between and among characters of various sexual orientations and numerical groupings). The smart, wonderfully trashy show ran for a shocking (in our modern streaming era) eight seasons, with a couple of regional remakes. Stream Elite on Netflix.

When pretty, popular girl Kate Wallis (Olivia Holt) goes missing without a trace in 1993, awkward Jeanette Turner (Chiara Aurelia) steps in to fill the gap, modeling herself after Kate by working her way into the missing girl's social circle and getting close with her boyfriend. That's all going great until Kate reappears two years later, accusing Jeanette of having witnessed the events around her disappearance and keeping quiet. Whoops. There's even more going on, as the show shifts back and forth between 1993, 1994, and 1995 to slowly reveal the missing pieces. Season two takes on a different story set in 1999 and 2000, and the forthcoming third season will shake things up again. Stream Cruel Summer on Hulu.

Teen drama at its finest and most bitchy, Gossip Girl follows the many scandals of a group of young Upper East Side socialites and hangers-on. The tangled teenage lives of Serena van der Woodsen (Blake Lively), her best frenemy Blair Waldorf (Leighton Meester), scholarship kid Dan Humphrey (Penn Badgley), and more pretty young boys and girls are chronicled in meticulous detail by the title's mysterious, omnipresent blogger Gossip Girl (voiced by Kristen Bell). It might seem slightly tame compared to The Shards, but the show carved a path nonetheless, scandalizing parents in the mid-aughts and hitting unhinged heights before its conclusion. (The two-season 2021 follow-up is also available on HBO Max.) Stream Gossip Girl on HBO Max and Netflix.

The tone is more insular than the glossy high school drama of The Shards, dealing primarily with pop culture's most disturbing mother-son relationship, but there's something very Ryan Murphy in the heightened operatic ickiness of it all. Freddie Highmore stars as Norman Bates (original author Robert Bloch having based the character on serial killer Ed Gein), with Vera Farmiga as his mother Norma (in her pre-dessicated-corpse days). Like a lot of media spun off from Alfred Hitchcock's seminal Psycho, it's better than it has any right to be, with compelling character development and several surprises, even if we already know more or less where it's all heading. Stream Bates Motel on Prime Video.

As utterly batshit on its own terms as The Shards (and then some), Riverdale is a wild take on the once entirely wholesome Archie comics universe, veering wildly between genres. At its outset, it's a coming-of-age teen drama for the visible-abs set, with a murder mystery and a student-teacher sex thing going on. There's plenty of that kind of thing before the weirder stuff comes into play, from supernatural shenanigans to alternate universes. Luckily, it knows what kind of show it is, and taking itself seriously in the face of absolutely bonkers plot twists is very much part of the fun. Steam Riverdale on Netflix.

An earlier bit of Ryan Murphy wackiness, this one is more of an overt satire—though with the over-the-top selections of the producer's oeuvre, the line between comedy and drama is always a little thin. Here we find the all-star line-up of Emma Roberts, Ariana Grande, Billie Lourd, and Abigail Breslin as sorority sisters facing down a threatening and downright vicious dean (Jamie Lee Curtis, in a flawless bit of casting) alongside a serial killer who dresses up like their school's Red Devil mascot, all of it tying in to some wild stuff that went on way back in 1995. Stream Scream Queens on Hulu.

title: Microsoft's Record-Setting Patch Tuesday Update Fixes Nearly 1,000 Flaws
description: Two of the vulnerabilities addressed this month are actively exploited zero-days.
fullText:
Security updates have been trending larger, and Microsoft's Patch Tuesday for September is no exception. The company just released fixes for nearly 1,000 bugs, which is approaching double the number of flaws patched in July (the previous record). Two of the vulnerabilities addressed this month are zero-days that have been exploited in the wild.

This massive jump is in large part due to AI, which is making it easier for bad actors to develop tools to exploit vulnerabilities while also allowing developers to find and fix them more quickly. This means we're likely to continue seeing sizeable updates on shorter release cycles, ideally reducing the time hackers have to take advantage of these flaws. Microsoft has typically pushed Patch Tuesday fixes around 10 a.m. PT on the second Tuesday of every month.

It's always been important to install security updates as soon as they're available, but it's even more critical now with a larger number of flaws open to exploitation. PC users should receive Patch Tuesday updates automatically, but you can check the status via Start > Settings > Windows Update > Check for Windows updates.

As BleepingComputer reports, the 966 flaws fixed this month are broken down across the following categories: 438 elevation-of-privilege vulnerabilities, 19 security feature bypass vulnerabilities, 258 remote-code-execution vulnerabilities, 173 information disclosure vulnerabilities, 16 spoofing vulnerabilities, and 56 denial-of-service vulnerabilities. These figures do not include other vulnerabilities (204 in total across other Microsoft products) patched earlier this month.

One of the zero-days addressed in September is an elevation of privilege vulnerability in the Windows Update Stack. CVE-2026-81963 allows attackers to gain SYSTEM privileges via improper link resolution before file access. The bug discovery has been attributed to Romain Deperne and the Microsoft Threat Intelligence Centre.

The other zero-day is also an elevation of privilege vulnerability. CVE-2026-85880 is a flaw in the Windows Advanced Local Procedure—an attacker could execute code in a low-privilege AppContainer, and the vulnerability could escape the sandbox and gain SYSTEM privileges locally. The bug was discovered by Volexity, as well as Mark Kelly, David Galazin, and Jeremy Hedges with Proofpoint.

Both zero-days have been actively exploited in the wild, though Microsoft has not provided any details as to how.

title: Apple Just Announced the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max
description: Apple's latest "Pro" iPhones are official.
fullText:
The iPhone Duo will inevitably steal tech headlines this week. After all, Apple finally made a foldable iPhone to compete with options from Samsung and Google. But while an iPhone with two displays is novel and exciting, it's also going to be expensive. I imagine there are many in the market for a new iPhone who aren't interested in spending as much as $2,000. There are also likely customers who don't want a foldable iPhone, and would prefer the standard smartphone design they're used to. That's where the iPhone 18 Pro comes in.

If you have an iPhone 17 Pro, you might confuse it for the iPhone 18 Pro. Indeed, Apple hasn't changed the overall design much this year, which is to be expected. The iPhone 17 Pro refreshed the Pro iPhone design with its large camera bump and plane of glass for MagSafe charging. The 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max aren't much different—though now the metal is color-matched to the back glass.

That being said, there are some changes here you may notice upon closer examination. Perhaps first you'd notice the 18 Pro's Dynamic Island is smaller than it has been on previous Pro iPhones. With it, you're able to run three tasks at once, rather than two. That may prove useful depending on what you're doing, or it may end up cluttering the top of your iPhone. 18 Pro users will have to be the judge. You'd also notice some new color options not available on the iPhone 17 Pro, which I'll cover below.

The displays will remain the same sizes as last year—6.3 inches on the iPhone 18 Pro, and 6.9 inches on the iPhone 18 Pro Max. But now, these displays use a more efficient LPTO+ technology.

Like the iPhone Duo, the iPhone 18 Pros come with Apple's new A20 Pro chip built on 2nm technology. The company touts how the new chip is great for processing AI on-device, with a six-core CPU, seven-core GPU, new Neural Accelerators, and a second Neural Engine. Apple focused on the A20 Pro's thermal cooling with the new vapor chamber in the 18 Pro. Apple says this means there are significant sustained performance improvements over the iPhone 17 Pro.

Apple says this chip has the fastest CPU in a smartphone, with 50% better memory bandwidth. But, as with all performance claims, we'll have to wait until testers try out the A20 Pro for themselves. Still, Apple's newest chips always improve on the previous generation by some degree, so it's safe to say the 18 Pro (and the Duo at that) will be the fastest iPhones yet.

Apple also says the iPhone 18 Pro has 36 hours of battery life while streaming video, while iPhone 18 Pro Max has 45 hours. The company says five minutes of charging gets you six hours of video playback.

Perhaps the biggest change for the iPhone 18 Pro this year is its cameras. Apple's Pro iPhones are known for their shooters, but for the 18 Pros, Apple has taken things up a notch. For the first time, these iPhones have variable apertures. When using the 48MP main camera, your iPhone can physically open and close its aperture to control how much light hits the sensor—up to 50% more light than before. That offers two benefits: In dim environments, you can let in more light than you normally could. You can also use the aperture to control the depth of field, or the background blur. A large aperture (more light) means a blurrier background, while a smaller aperture (less light) means a cleaner background.

Apple also introduced Pro Controls, which has been sorely missing on the iPhone. You now can control white balance and shutter speed, and check the histogram. This mode works for both photography and videography. There's now a new "smart focus tracking" feature that uses AI to keep focus on a subject. Photographic Styles get some additional upgrades and controls, and Time-Lapse also supports 4K. With the 18 Pro, Apple is rolling out a "reference" feature to ensure that an original shot can be confirmed if an edit is later made with AI. Apple calls this a "digital negative."

As previously mentioned, the iPhone 18 Pro's colors may be one of the most recognisably "new" features of this generation. Apple is rolling out color options in "Burgundy," "Glacier," and Silver, though the first two may be the more distinct of the bunch. Still, it's more variation than we have on the Duo.

Everything is getting more expensive, thanks to RAMaggedon, and the iPhone 18 Pro is no exception. Apple is raising the starting price this year to $1,199 for the 256GB model, while the iPhone 18 Pro Max starts at $1,299 for the 256GB variant.

Apple says the iPhone 18 Pro will be available to preorder on Saturday, Sept. 12 at 12 a.m. PT (3 a.m. ET). The devices then go on sale Friday, Sept. 18.

title: Where’s the iPhone 18?
description: Apple is giving its iPhone release schedule the biggest shake-up in history.
fullText:
There was something different about today's "Surprise and Shine" launch event from Apple: We didn't get the unveiling of the iPhone 18.

For the first time since Apple started releasing multiple iPhones per year, which was 2013 with the arrival of the iPhone 5c and the iPhone 5s (simpler times), we have several pro-level handsets without the standard version to accompany them. So what's behind the shift? And is the iPhone 18 canceled? Apple, predictably, isn't saying, but we've got enough clues to make an informed guess.

If you've been keeping up with Apple rumors since the launch of the iPhone 17, you'll know that this has long been predicted—notably by the most respected purveyor of Apple leaks in the business, reporter Mark Gurman. Gurman was predicting in Bloomberg as far back as November 2025 that we would only get the iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max, and the folding iPhone Duo in 2026.

The reason? According to Gurman, it's to spread out revenue more evenly across the year, rather than having most of the iPhones unveiled every September. It also takes some of the pressure off Apple's marketing teams and reduces the likelihood of mishaps like that Siri AI upgrade—which was announced way before it was ready. Gurman also went on record as saying that this is likely to be the norm for "years to come," so get used to it.

However, Gurman wasn't the first to break the news. In May of 2025, Wayne Ma at The Information reported that Apple would hold the standard iPhone 18 model over until 2027, based on conversations with anonymous supply chain sources. As per that report, one of the motivations behind the shift was to make more space for the folding iPhone, which makes sense considering it's Apple's first attempt at the form factor.

Just a day later, well-known and usually well-informed Apple analyst Ming-Chi Kuo backed up the story, saying that we'd see the foldable iPhone, the iPhone 18 Pro, the iPhone 18 Pro Max, and the iPhone Air 2 (then called the iPhone 18 Slim) in September 2026. Apart from that last handset, he was right.

Kuo added an extra reason for the shift as well: Competition from phone manufacturers based in Asia. A lot of these manufacturers release their flagship handsets during the first half of the year, including Samsung, and as far as Apple is concerned, that can leave it playing catch-up by the time September rolls around.

While the iPhone 18 was a no-show at the "Surprise and Shine" event, there's no indication that it's been canceled. Apple still wants to cater to those who'd rather spend a little less on their iPhones (the iPhone 18 Pro starts at $1,119), and the most educated guesses we've seen suggest we'll get the base version of the phone sometime in March.

It's unlikely to be on its own either. We're also expecting to see the iPhone 18e and the iPhone Air 2 appear at the same time, following on from the iPhone 17e (launched in March 2026) and the original iPhone Air (launched in September 2025, alongside the iPhone 17 series).

And that "e" phone series set the foundation for the calendar shift we've now seen with the standard iPhone 18 model. The first of these more affordable handsets, the iPhone SE, showed up in March 2016—it was then followed by the iPhone SE 2 (April 2020), the iPhone SE 3 (March 2022), and the iPhone 16e (February 2025). That shows Apple has been eyeing up the February-March-April slot for non-pro-level iPhones for a decade at this point.

The rumors so far suggest the iPhone 18 will use an A20 chipset, while we're likely to get a RAM bump as well. We now know that the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max have a smaller Dynamic Island, with the ability to show up to three Live Activities, and that's something that should carry across to the standard model (along with iOS 27).

Apple didn't mention the iPhone 18 at all today—not even in a post-credits sequence—but it would be a major surprise if the handset didn't make a belated appearance sometime in the first quarter of next year. If this is the iPhone that's for you, you're just going to have to wait a little while longer.

title: The iPhone 18 Pro Series Comes With Big Gains in Battery Life
description: Finally, a standard iPhone Pro model with the battery we're used to on a Pro Max.
fullText:
While the iPhone 18 Pro looks similar to last year's model, the internals are a different story. The new A20 Pro processor with 32 Neural Engine cores will go a long way helping with on-device AI tasks—but you might not feel those differences all the time.

The new updates to battery life and charging, however, will make an actual difference in daily use on the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max. Apple is promising the best battery life on an iPhone yet, and is finally supporting faster wired charging.

According to Apple, the regular sized iPhone 18 Pro will have the same battery life as the outgoing, larger iPhone 17 Pro Max model, which is quite a big deal. Apple is combining the efficiency gains in the A20 Pro chip with new battery technology to deliver this large leap in battery life.

You will get 45 hours of video playback on the iPhone 18 Pro Max, and 36 hours on the iPhone 18 Pro model. The iPhone 18 Pro will last 24 hours per charge, while the 18 Pro Max can go up to 30 hours.

According to Apple, this is based on tests performed with Apple's 40W Dynamic Power Adapter with a 60W max charging speed. Wired fast charging is also supported with 60W-capable USB-C cables and USB PD 3.1 adapters that support Adjustable Voltage Supply.

The world of Android flagships is filled with quick-charging smartphones, and some of that clout will now come over to the iPhone as well. A quick five-minute wired charge will give you up to six hours of video playback, and more importantly, you get 50% charging in just 15 minutes. Even wireless charging is faster, with 50% charging in around 30 minutes.

title: Apple Just Announced the Foldable 'iPhone Duo'
description: It's Apple's first foldable smartphone.
fullText:
Since Apple announced the date of its big September event, we've expected the company to reveal the "iPhone Ultra," its first foldable smartphone. As it turns out, half of that prediction came true: While the company did indeed showcase the first iPhone to transform from smartphone to tablet, it isn't actually called the Ultra. Instead, the company surprised us all with a new name: iPhone Duo.

It's immediately apparent that the iPhone Duo has a much different design than any iPhone Apple has ever made. This device is foldable, which means it has two functioning displays, depending on how you use it. When closed, the Duo has a funkier 5.4-inch display than the one you might be used to on an iPhone, but it's fully functional. You don't actually have to open up the Duo to use it: You can text, browse Safari, play games, and do whatever you normally would on your iPhone from here. The selfie cam and two rear cameras mean you can take FaceTime calls and shoot photos and videos while the Duo is in this position. If you never wanted to open up your Duo, you would probably never have to.

Open it up, however, and you'll be greeted by a much larger 7.6-inch display. This is the benefit of foldable smartphones: You have access to a mini tablet (sometimes called a "phablet") whenever you want it. That extra screen real estate means you can view single apps in a much larger window, but also run two apps side-by-side. That's a first for any iPhone, even if it's not a first for smartphones in general. And because this is a tablet-like display, your Home Screen looks a bit more like an iPad's, complete with extra widgets and a macOS-like Dock. There's even a Dock on the outer display, and many controls are adjusted to sit on the right of the display to make them accessible using your thumb.

Interestingly, the Duo is the first iPhone in years to lack Face ID. Instead, this device marks the return of Touch ID, integrated into the Side button. (You can also unlock it with your Apple Watch.) It also supports Apple Pencil for the first time on iPhone, and includes two batteries, providing 31 hours of video playback on the inner display, and 44 hours on the outer. You can reach 50% battery in 20 minutes of charging, and five hours of use after five minutes.

It works in many different orientations: You can stand it up tent-style or like a laptop, or fold it slightly to split your keyboard. It also works in StandBy by folding it on its side.

Like the iPhone 18 Pros, the iPhone Duo comes with Apple's new A20 Pro chip. But for the Duo, the chip has a new display engine to power both screens. Apple says it offers up to 35% faster performance than iPhone 17 Pro. While I'm sure it's Apple's fastest chip yet, we'll have to wait until independent benchmarkers put it to the test to know how much better it is than the A19 Pro. The Duo also has Apple's proprietary C2 modem, which provides faster uploads and quicker reconnection to networks.

As noted above, the iPhone Duo has four cameras: two rear cameras and two selfie cameras. Let's start with those rear cameras: Apple has a 48MP fusion lens and a 2x telephoto lens. Some might be sad about the omission of an ultrawide lens. At the same time, the Duo might not be the iPhone for users who care most about mobile photography. Perhaps it'll feel more like the cameras on the iPad: useful to have, but not exactly a selling point. Like the 18 Pro, the Duo supports 4K Time-Lapses and new Photographic Styles.

Perhaps more importantly, the Duo has two selfie cameras: one on the front display, and one on the inner display. This ensures that you can take FaceTime calls and selfies in whichever orientation you have the iPhone Duo in. Crucially, the inner camera is embedded in the display, so you don't ever see it. There are a lot of camera perks with those dual displays: Your subject can see themselves in the outer display; you can stand up the Duo like a tripod; and you can project FaceTime calls on both displays, so everyone can see who you're talking to.

Apple didn't go all out with the colors for the Duo. Buyers will only have two options to choose from here: Star White or Night Sky (dark blue). That's in contrast to the iPhone 18 Pro, which comes in four interesting colors. That said, I'm guessing Apple doesn't expect Duo sales to be affected by color options: Buyers are either going to pay up for the Duo, or they're not, and fun colors probably wouldn't play into that conversation.

Apple's first foldable iPhone doesn't come cheap, of course. The iPhone Duo officially starts at $1,999, which makes this the most expensive iPhone Apple has ever made. And yet, that doesn't sound so bad: Initial reports suggested that the Duo would be more than $2,000, which seemed quite believable considering how RAMaggedon is driving the costs up for all types of tech.

The iPhone Duo can be more expensive, however. $1,999 is the starting price for the 256GB model, though it goes up to 2TB.

While Apple announced the iPhone Duo today, it won't be available right away. Instead, the company says preorders begin Oct. 16, while sales begin Oct. 23. While iPhone preorders are usually a frantic affair, I imagine the Duo's demand will be historic. If you're interested in picking one up as soon as possible, you'll likely want to make sure you preorder it as soon as Apple lets you.

title: Apple's 'Reference Image' Preserves Your Original Photos (Even After You Edit Them)
description: You can think of it like a permanenet digital photo negative.
fullText:
Figuring out what’s real online is only getting harder, and AI watermarks can only go so far to identify fakes. But today, Apple introduced a new standard to at least help identify real images taken directly on an iPhone: Apple Reference Image. It won’t solve the problem of finding the truth online, but it could be a helpful tool towards that goal.

The new feature will be available on iPhone 18 Pro models to start. It works by taking signed sensor data from the camera and using it to create a reference picture that can’t be edited, alongside a version that can be changed. The idea here is to give you a version of the picture that’s authenticated at the moment of capture, which you can compare against any modified versions later.

This provenance metadata can be preserved through certain supported sharing methods, which for now means select other Apple devices can check their verification status. That doesn’t mean that anyone can check the veracity of an image—especially if the version that gets posted and shared is an edited variant—but it provides a tool for the person or organization that took the picture originally to offer proof of verification.

This tool comes alongside the announcement that Apple will soon add support for the SynthID standard. This will potentially help users identify when an image has been created or modified with AI. Apple joins a long (though not exactly comprehensive) list of major tech companies to support the standard, including OpenAI, Nvidia, and obviously Google, the original creator of SynthID.

We’re still in the midst of a scattershot image verification ecosystem. Apple’s Reference Image is a clever implementation that gives the end user a signed original to compare a picture against, which is a step up from C2PA metadata that merely embeds information about an image’s origin. It’s still unclear how widely these verification tools will be implemented and how easy it will be for users to trace where an image comes from and how, precisely, it was modified, but still, something is better than nothing.

title: Why the Apple Health App's Redesign Is a Big Deal
description: We've needed this dashboard for years.
fullText:
Apple announced new watches today—a Series 12 and an Ultra 4—which you can read more about here. But alongside the watch features, Apple announced a revamped Health app. We’ll soon have a proper dashboard for health data and insights, rivaling what you can get from the companion apps for other wearables like Whoop, Garmin, and Fitbit.

Apple was an early trendsetter when it came to health-focused watches, but it quickly fell behind as all the other devices began adding sleep scores, recovery scores, and customized insights based on your day’s data. If you open up a good wearable app, you’ll instantly know what’s going on with your body’s data and what you should probably do about it. I’m often skeptical of the specifics—you shouldn’t read too much into any app’s metrics—but it’s good to have something to look at.

The Apple Health app has existed for years, but it’s mostly a dry listing of data from different sources. Which is a shame, because it has access to an incredible amount of data, not to mention powerful hidden features that most of us never manage to discover.

Last year, Apple finally revamped its Fitness app to match what other wearables give us in terms of activity tracking. This year, we finally get the other half: a Health app that can tell you how well you slept, how “recovered” you are, and how your long-term health seems to be shaping up.

Although Apple showed these features in the context of an Apple Watch upgrade (more on that below), the things that intrigue me most are likely to be software updates that roll out to iPhones in general. That’s my guess, in any case—I’ll watch Apple’s announcements 

Apple showed a new Readiness score, which can tell you whether you need to “recover,” should “pace yourself,” are “ready,” or should “go for it.” (That’s in order from worst to best.) This score can update during the day, making it a more readable version of something like Garmin’s Body Battery.

When you open your Health app, it looks like relevant “insights” will show up at the top of the screen, including your sleep, recovery, and rings, and the main screen can show your sleep from the past night along with a sleep score. The app includes text summaries and guidance that are generated by Apple Intelligence, suggesting that you'll need an iPhone 16 or later for these.

In the screenshots Apple shared, I spied a tiny number that is actually a huge change of focus for the company: one of the insights shows your rings next to your step count for the day. Apple has never made a big deal about steps, to the point where people often download third-party step counters to be able to easily view steps on the watch. But the Health app has kept count all along, and now that number is showing up somewhere you can easily see it.

Depending on how well Apple executes this idea, I could see apps like Bevel becoming obsolete. And Bevel already makes some wearables’ apps (like Google Health) obsolete—you can just read the data from Bevel, or now Apple Health, instead of using the app that comes with your Fitbit. Other fitness tech companies will now have a serious competitor that is available for free on customers’ phones.

I roll my eyes every time a health or fitness app claims to gauge my “longevity” or some true “age” of my body. Depending on which app you ask, I’m either 10 years younger than I really am, or three years older.

Apple has joined the club, with a whole Longevity tab in the Health app. (That now brings the number of tabs to three: the main screen, the sharing tab, and now longevity in the middle.) Despite the eye-rolling, I see what Apple is doing here. Don’t think of longevity in this (or any) app as being an accurate gauge of how long you will live; think of it as how your long-term health habits are adding up. Apple’s longevity calculations involve seven areas, with icons indicating something like nutrition, exercise, heart health, hearing health, movement (maybe steps), sleep, and mental well-being.

There’s also a new set of assessments, including a VO2max assessment. According to Apple’s presentation, you’ll prop your phone up where it can see your full body, and then you’ll step to a metronome’s beat, speeding up as the beeps speed up until you’re running in place. This sounds like it may have been inspired by the Harvard step test, which has you step up and down in place and then measure your heart rate. Until now, Apple’s VO2max estimates have always been based on GPS-tracked activities like outdoor running. (Apple finished in the middle of the pack when I tested the accuracy of nine devices’ VO2max estimates. I’m curious to see whether the new assessment does better.)

When it comes to the full experience—with the Apple Watch itself—there’s a notable upgrade to the Series 12 Apple Watch compared to previous versions. Apple has redesigned the heart rate sensor on the back of the watch, with larger lights and redesigned photodiodes to detect the reflected light.

With these redesigns, Apple says it has the “most accurate heart rate sensing in a wearable.” To which I say: I’ll believe it when I see it. In my testing over the past few years, Apple Watches have lagged well behind other wearables’ heart rate sensors when I test them for accuracy. I’d certainly believe that it found room for improvement, but is the new Apple sensor really going to be able to beat Garmin’s fifth-generation sensor, the one that made me do a double take because I thought I had it mixed up with my chest strap data?

Apple has released a whitepaper with the results of an internal heart rate accuracy study it did comparing the Series 12 (but not the Ultra 4) against the Garmin Forerunner 970, Google Pixel Watch 4, Huawei Watch 5, Samsung Galaxy Watch 8, Whoop 5.0, and Oura Ring 5, with a Polar H10 chest strap for reference. It's a short paper, and doesn't show the kind of detail I would like to see from a thorough test, so you can bet I'll be investigating this myself once I get my hands on the new watch. If Apple really reaches a Forerunner 970 level of accuracy, I’ll be incredibly impressed.

title: We Finally Know iOS 27's Release Date
description: Here's when you can install iOS 27 on your iPhone.
fullText:
Apple's September event was a big one. The company announced the new iPhone 18 Pro, Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4, AirPods 5, and the foldable iPhone Duo. While the company certainly highlighted numerous software features for each of these devices, including some never-before-seen health features for Apple Watch, this was very much a hardware event. That's no surprise, of course: Apple reserves the vast majority of its software news for WWDC in June. But despite that fact, there was one particularly big piece of software news to come out of September's keynote: iOS 27's release date.

Since Apple is using iOS 27 to advertise many of the capabilities of its upcoming devices, it makes sense that the company would need to give an ETA for the update. After all, the iPhone 18 Pro launches on Friday, Sept. 18, running iOS 27. The update would presumably need to be out by then, unless Apple intended iPhone 18 Pro users to be the first of its user base to run the software. (Spoilers: it did not intend that.)

As it happens, the company officially announced the update's launch date, though it didn't advertise it heavily. At the bottom of its newsroom posts for each of its new product announcements, the company confirmed that iOS 27 will launch on Monday, Sept. 14. Developers have been beta testing iOS 27 since June, and Apple opened up the public beta one month later. Since then, volunteers have been trialing Apple's upcoming features, including Siri AI, new image editing tools, and dual-capture during FaceTime calls.

Apple also confirmed that watchOS 27 will launch on Sept. 14 as well. However, at this time, it isn't clear whether Apple's other software updates, such as macOS 27 Golden Gate and iPadOS 27, will also launch at this time. If I had to guess, I would say these updates will arrive in tandem, especially iPadOS 27, but we'll have to wait for Apple's confirmation to know for sure.

Apple is supporting a long list of iPhones with iOS 27, going all the way back to 2019's iPhone 11 series. The full list is as follows:

iPhone SE (2nd generation and later)

That said, some features are only available on certain iPhone models. Apple Intelligence (including Siri AI) is only accessible on iPhone 15 Pro and newer. Certain AI features, like Siri voice customization, is only available on iPhone 17 Pro and newer, including iPhone Air.

title: Why the iPhone 18 Pro's Variable Aperture Is a Big Development for Smartphone Photography
description: Variable aperture is a huge development for smartphone photography.
fullText:
Every year, Apple claims its newly launched iPhones have the best cameras ever, and those improvements usually revolve around improved sensors, lenses, and software updates. This year, though, there's an unusual camera upgrade that's going to make a massive difference to your photos and videos: The iPhone 18 Pro and the iPhone 18 Pro Max have a variable-aperture lens, a feature unavailable on the much more expensive iPhone Duo. Variable aperture gives you far greater control over lighting in your iPhone photos.

A camera's aperture lets you control how much light reaches the lens. For a brighter photo, you want to let in more light; for a darker one, you'd ideally let in less. This system is similar to the pupils of your eyes, which constrict when the light is too bright and dilate when you suddenly go from bright sunshine to a dark room.

In DSLR cameras, you can see overlapping blades that partially cover the lens. This opening increases or decreases in size depending on the aperture value. This technology is expensive to implement in a smartphone lens, and so far, the improvement in photos hasn't been good enough to justify the investment. That's why it's rare to find the feature in most phones. Apple added variable aperture to its smartphones for the first time with the launch of the iPhone 18 Pro series. (Note that aperture values are denoted in f-numbers, which means that when you adjust a camera's aperture, the value looks something like f/1.8, f/4.0, etc. The lower the f-number, the brighter the image becomes.)

The iPhone 18 Pro has three rear cameras, but only the main camera offers a variable aperture. It's a 48-megapixel sensor with four aperture f-numbers supported. You can pick an aperture value from f/1.48, f/1.8, f/2.8, and f/4.0m, which should make it significantly easier to get the exposure just right in difficult lighting conditions. You'll also be able to take better photos in low light and try a few additional creative shots with your iPhone 18 Pro. Having a variable aperture is great for controlling depth of field, so you can easily blur the background or keep it in sharp focus when you take photos.

With a larger aperture (f/1.48), you'll be able to reduce the depth of field and blur the background for shots that require focus on a single subject. You can use a smaller aperture (f/4.0) to capture stunning landscapes, where you want the entire photo to be in focus.

If you're thinking that your iPhone already does these things, you're sort of right. But it's worth remembering that up until now, iPhones had to rely on software to perform these tasks, which gets the job done, but the results aren't always exactly what you'd visualize. Having hardware control over aperture gives you greater control over the output and brings the final result much closer to what you visualized. In theory, variable aperture should make the iPhone 18 Pro better for astrophotography, too, but until all of these tasks are tested, it's hard to say how much impact the new feature will have.

title: Ryder Cup race a 'big part' of Lowry's motivation
description: Shane Lowry says it is time to get himself "in gear" if he is to secure his spot on Europe's Ryder Cup team for Adare Manor next year.
fullText:
Shane Lowry says it is time to get himself "in gear" if he is to secure his spot on Europe's Ryder Cup team for Adare Manor next year.

The 2019 Open champion is in the field at the Irish Open this week, with the qualification process for the 2027 Ryder Cup, to be held in County Limerick from 17-19 September, having commenced last month.

Irishman Lowry was a member of the European teams in 2021, 2023 and 2025, holing the winning putt in the latter event at Bethpage Black.

The 39-year-old has, however, fallen from 26th to 53rd in the world rankings over the course of 2026 in a season characterised by frustrating near-misses.

While Lowry said performing well in front of an Irish crowd at Doonbeg this week would always be a "carrot dangling", there is an added significance knowing each tournament between now and next August could bring him closer to the long-held goal of playing in a Ryder Cup on home soil.

"When that was announced, you look at the dates, look at how old you'll be, and that's been a big big goal of mine," Lowry told BBC Sport NI's Stephen Watson.

"To be part of a home Ryder Cup team is amazing, but to be part of one in Ireland would be very, very cool.

"It goes without saying, Ryder Cup points have started so it's time to get myself in gear and get on that team. That's going to be a big part of my motivation over the next 12 months."

Irish Open will feel 'different' with Trump visit

'Time will tell' - Rahm on LIV Golf future

Lowry is one of seven players from the victorious 2025 team who will be teeing it up at the Irish Open this week.

With Adare Manor just 60 miles from Doonbeg, Europe captain Luke Donald has arranged a meeting of 16 prospective team members at the first Irish course to stage the biennial event since the K Club in 2006.

Among the group will be potential Ryder Cup rookies Alex Fitzpatrick, Eugenio Chacarra, Kristoffer Reitan and Angel Ayora, although Donald is also keen to get more experienced players acquainted with a venue best known for staging the JP McManus Pro-Am.

"I did some off how strong some of the guys are playing statistically and a few of my own picks," said Donald of how he decided on the group that will gather on Sunday and Monday.

"I think it's just an opportunity to see the course. Eight or nine of the guys have never played it. The more we can get out and familiarise ourselves, it'll stand us in good stead."

Donald feels the demise of LIV Golf could potentially make his selection process more straightforward this time around.

The Englishman, who first became captain for the 2023 event after planned skipper Henrik Stenson switched to the breakaway tour, had LIV players Tyrrell Hatton and Jon Rahm in his team last year, although he had to use a wildcard pick on the latter.

After LIV filed for bankruptcy protection in the US on Tuesday, players are now free to leave rather than see out their contracts and the DP World Tour has already said there has been a "high volume" of interest.

That could mean prospective team members playing in a greater number of events where Ryder Cup points are on offer.

"I think you always want the six guys who qualify automatically to be the strongest," Donald added.

"If that's Jon and Tyrrell playing more and playing more here where the points are, that gives them more opportunities to qualify. That's a good thing."

title: Grand Canyon water supply to be restored in weeks, not months
description: National Park Service officials expect to restore a reliable water supply in the Grand Canyon in weeks — not months — as the deadly flash flood didn’t damage most of a near-complete pipeline project, ...
fullText:
PHOENIX (AP) — National Park Service officials expect to restore a reliable water supply in the Grand Canyon in weeks — not months — as the deadly flash flood didn't damage most of a near-complete pipeline project, they said Tuesday.

Officials said that they were just over a month away from completing a major upgrade to the sole 12.5-mile-long (20-kilometer) Transcanyon Waterline, which supplied water for millions of visitors to the Grand Canyon's South Rim and about 1,600 residents of Grand Canyon Village.

Construction of a temporary water intake that matches the park's pre-flood pumping capacity will start this week. Park officials encourage residents and tourists to continue conserving water as they work on a more than $200 million repair and upgrade project.

Before the floods, officials said the project would ensure the park can meet its water supply needs for the next 50 years or more.

"The damage to this old pipe is no longer relevant to our new solution," Dave Black, deputy incident commander at the National Park Service's Western Incident Management Team, said. "Every gallon we conserve gives our crews more time to complete the work in the canyon."

The flash flood on Aug. 29 caused two deaths, left one person missing and caused about 80 rescues. Search and rescue efforts are ongoing.

The floods mark the third time that overnight stays have been paused due to pipeline failures since August 2024.

Officials also implemented significant water conservation measures for residents to protect the limited stored water on the South Rim, where most visitors go.

Gloria Barrett, a longtime resident of Grand Canyon Village who works for a helicopter tour company, shut off her water heater to help her household of four conserve water.

"That inhibits us from taking longer showers because the water's so cold, which is miserable," she said.

Barrett, her partner and his two teenage sons have been eating on paper plates to avoid doing dishes and reusing cooking water to give to their dog. In her 10 years living inside the park, Barrett said she has learned to get creative with water conservation — the pipeline has broken more than 85 times since 2010 — but she has never seen damage this "extreme."

The pipeline, which has been in place nearly twice as long as it was supposed to be, crosses rugged terrain from the quieter South Rim, down to the canyon floor and back up to the South Rim to provide drinking water and fire suppression.

Many families in Grand Canyon Village live paycheck to paycheck, Barrett said, and leaving "is not an option for us — it's not feasible." But for the 27-year-old, who also owns a transport company that shuttles tourists from rim to rim, the hotel closures brought a wave of cancellations during what she said was her busiest season.

Bing Pan, a tourism and recreation professor at Pennsylvania State University, said tourism also supports the largely part-time, seasonal workforce on the South Rim. Even weeks of slowed service could be detrimental to their families.

"Workers in the park, who are paid around $15 to $20 per hour, usually don't have much savings," Pan said. "Natural disasters and slowed service flows could push them to the brink of leaving the area, devastating the local tourism economy."

This story has been corrected to show the meeting was Tuesday, not Wednesday.

Schoenbaum reported from Salt Lake City.

title: Hants beat Blaze to boost One-Day Cup final hopes
description: Hampshire beat The Blaze while Somerset, Surrey and Essex also win in race to One-Day Cup final.
fullText:
Hampshire gave themselves a chance of going straight through to the Women's One-Day Cup final with a seven-wicket victory over The Blaze.

Maia Bouchier's superb 118, her fourth century of the summer, helped Hampshire chase a target of 250 inside 40 overs.

That gave them the extra bonus point to bring them level with The Blaze at the top of the table having completed their 16 group matches.

If the Nottingham based team lose their last group game against Essex on Friday, Hampshire will qualify for the final on 19 September and The Blaze will have to play an eliminator against the team that finishes third in the table.

Despite losing to this season's other form side in Southampton, The Blaze are still heavy favourites to reach their third final in 2026.

They only need to pick up one point against Essex on Friday to make the One-Day Cup showpiece.

Against Hampshire, a number of Blaze batters struggled to kick on after making good starts. Opener Tammy Beaumont top scored with 56 and they finished on 249-7.

Bouchier and Ella McCaughan set the hosts on their way in the chase with an opening stand of 98 before a second-wicket partnership of 116 with Abi Norgrove (52) took Hampshire to 214-1.

Norgrove was dismissed by Grace Ballinger and Bouchier went soon after to Cassidy McCarthy, having struck 16 fours in her 107-ball innings, but the job was already done.

Elsewhere Surrey maintained their hopes of reaching next Wednesday's eliminator as they bowled Warwickshire out for 55 in a 10-wicket victory.

Kate Coppack tore through the Bears batting line-up with 5-22 before Rachel King (41 not out) and Alice Monaghan took Surrey to 59-0 in 10.2 overs.

Somerset also stayed in with a chance of finishing third in the group with a five-wicket win over Lancashire.

Seren Smale's 82 helped Lancashire to 240-9, but a composed unbeaten 77 by Jess Hazell took Somerset home with 13 balls to spare.

Somerset are a point behind third-placed Surrey with both sides facing each other in their final group fixture on Saturday at The Oval. The loser will be knocked out of the competition.

Wednesday's final game saw the table's bottom two sides, Essex and Yorkshire, meet at Chelmsford with the hosts picking up an eight-run victory.

Essex, led by 87 from captain Grace Scrivens, were bowled out for 241 but Yorkshire could only make 233 all out in reply.

title: Hermann equals ODI debut score record in SA win
description: Jordan Hermann strikes 150 to equal the record for the highest score in a one-day international debut as South Africa beat Namibia by 99 runs in Windhoek.
fullText:
First one-day international, Windhoek

South Africa 348-6 (50 overs): Hermann 150 (126), De Zorzi 72 (84); Trumpelmann 4-68

Nambia 162-8 (31 overs): Kruger 34 (60); Subrayen 4-29

South Africa won by 99 runs (DLS method) and lead the three-match series 1-0

Jordan Hermann struck 150 to equal the record for the highest score in a one-day international debut as South Africa beat Namibia by 99 runs in Windhoek.

The opener's 126-ball innings saw him draw level with compatriot Matthew Breetzke, who scored 150 from 148 deliveries against New Zealand in February 2025.

Hermann put on a 167-ball second-wicket partnership of 190 with Tony de Zorzi (70), hitting 17 fours and three sixes across his innings.

The 24-year-old reached his first fifty off 61 balls but his next two half-centuries came off 32 deliveries apiece.

Having reached 150 with a single in the covers, he was dismissed from the following delivery, caught at deep-midwicket by Louren Steenkamp off the bowling of seamer Ruben Trumpelmann (4-68) to leave his side on 275-3 in the 42nd over.

South Africa added a further 73 runs to finish on 348-6 having been put into bat but lost Jordan's older brother Ruben, playing in his second ODI, for eight when he trapped lbw by Trumpelmann.

Nambia's chase was affected by rain delays and was ultimately reduced to 31 overs, with the hosts falling well short of their target of 262, revised by the Duckworth-Lewis-Stern method.

They closed on 162-8, with opener Malan Kruger top-scoring with 34, while South Africa spinner Prenelan Subrayen finished with figures of 4-29.

South Africa's win, in the first ODI encounter between the neighbouring countries, sees them go 1-0 up in the three-matches series with further fixtures to follow at the same ground on Friday and Sunday (both 08:30 BST).

The visitors have named a rotated squad for the series, with Hermann, who has made six T20 appearances for South Africa, one of three debutants in this match alongside Connor Esterhuizen and Duan Jansen.

The reserve-heavy line-up won four of their five matches in a T20 tri-series against Namibia and Zimbabwe that preceded the ODIs, with Hermann playing every fixture alongside Ruben and top-scoring with 53 in Sunday's final.

He has not been selected for South Africa's next assignment, a home series of three ODIs and three Tests against Australia, starting later this month.

Notifications, social media and more with BBC Sport

title: Trump says oil prices that spiked because of Iran war likely won't come down until after midterms
description: President Donald Trump said Wednesday that oil prices that have surged because of the Iran war likely won’t come down until after U.S. midterm elections.  Oil prices on Wednesday jumped more than 3%, ...
fullText:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump said Wednesday that oil prices that have surged because of the Iran war likely won't come down until after U.S. midterm elections.

Oil prices on Wednesday jumped more than 3%, pushing international Brent crude past the $100 threshold for the first time since July as salvos between the U.S. and Iran escalated.

"Right after the election, oil prices are going to be tumbling downward," Trump said. "I think it's going to take a little bit longer than the midterm."

Trump, in an exchange with reporters before traveling to Dallas for the midterm Republican convention, added that he believes Iran will finally relent after the pivotal elections are held in the U.S.

"They're desperate to try and affect the election, so that we can get a nice weak group of people in there, and leave them alone and let them have their nuclear weapon," Trump said. He added, "I think the war's going to end immediately after the election because they can't hold out any longer," Trump said.

The president at the outset of the war said it would last a matter of weeks. The conflict is now in its seventh month. The U.S.-Israel war against Iran has led to a dramatic slowdown of Gulf oil moving through the Strait of Hormuz, which about 20% of the world's petroleum passed through prior to the conflict.

The comments were a striking acknowledgment from Trump about the status of the conflict as his Republican administration faces mounting pressure to address high gas prices as the war in Iran grinds on with no conclusion in sight.

Trump last week downplayed the conflict as "small potatoes" even as Republicans expressed concern the war will loom large with voters left navigating elevated gas prices and higher inflation.

The U.S. has tapped its strategic petroleum reserves, which in early August fell below 300 million barrels, down by more than 100 million barrels since the start of 2026.

Trump's prediction that the war won't be wrapped up until after Nov. 3 comes after Vice President JD Vance last week steered clear of predicting that the conflict would be over by the midterm elections, in which Republicans are trying to hang on to their narrow majorities in Congress.

Vance told reporters he didn't want to set "artificial timelines" for the war's end.

"But when you ask, 'When will this end?' You're asking me a question like, 'When will the Iranians stop shooting at ships?'" Vance said. "I think the reality is, I don't know the answer to that question. You would have to ask the Iranians."

U.S. benchmark crude on Wednesday stood at around $96 a barrel, and U.S. gasoline prices rose sharply overnight.

The average price for a gallon of regular gasoline ticked up 7 cents overnight t o hit $4.22, now more than a dollar above what it cost at this point last year, according to AAA.

Diesel prices, which can have an outsize impact on consumers because it is used in shipping and production, hit an all-time high Friday and have continued to climb since. The average price per gallon rose to $5.94 overnight, up 9 cents from Friday.

Jet fuel has become so expensive that U.S. and international carriers have cut flights while raising fares and fees.

The latest market gyrations come after the U.S. military reported striking five Iranian tankers in response to attempted missile attacks on a Navy warship and after attacks by an Iranian-backed Houthi rebel group ignited fires at oil facilities in Saudi Arabia.

AP writer Cathy Bussewitz contributed reporting.

title: ‘Nothing adds up’: Mica Miller’s last conversation with divorce attorney
description: Miller was found dead in April 2024 and her case has brought national attention after the release of Netflix series “Death of the Pastor’s Wife."
fullText:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=G5ShdCcUFvA

(NewsNation) — The divorce attorney for Mica Miller, who was found dead in what was ruled at a suicide at a state park last year, is speaking out about their final conversation and why "nothing adds up."

"It doesn't make any sense to me," Regina Ward told NewsNation's Brian Entin. "And then, of course, as time passed, nothing added up for me, just like everybody else that's looked at all the different aspects of the case."

Miller was found dead in April 2024 and her case has brought national attention after the Netflix series "Death of the Pastor's Wife" was released.

There is an ongoing case against her estranged husband Pastor John-Paul Miller for cyberstalking and making false statements — though there is no evidence he is involved directly in her death.

Suspicion has surrounded Miller since his wife's death, even though authorities ruled it a suicide. He faces separate federal charges tied to cyberstalking and making false statements to investigators.

Ward also told Entin she has more unreleased recordings with JP Miller — beyond what viewers of the Netflix show have heard.

"There's more than one call, by the way. There's more than one call," she said. "I have more than one recording with John Paul Miller."

Ward said she believed JP was attempting to control the narrative surrounding his wife's death and potentially win Ward's support.

"He was just so dying to get to talk to me. And the reason that he was dying to talk to me primarily is because he knows my stance on this. He knows I know what he is. He just thought that if he could convince attorney Regina Ward and get me on his side, my God, what a powerful tool that would have been for him," Ward said.

"But I saw all that stuff coming," she added.

title: Joe Biden shares health update after prostate cancer diagnosis while issuing warning to others
description: Joe Biden revealed his radiation treatment from last fall "worked as intended" as he urged men to discuss prostate cancer screening with their doctors.
fullText:
Former President Joe Biden shared an update on his battle with prostate cancer Tuesday, revealing that radiation treatment he underwent last fall "worked as intended" while urging American men not to delay conversations with their doctors about cancer screening.

Biden, 83, issued the update in a lengthy social media post marking Prostate Cancer Awareness Month, saying the occasion was more personal for him following his diagnosis last year.

"The radiation treatment from last fall worked as intended, and I continue to do the things I care about, like finishing my memoir," Biden wrote.

Jill Biden Says Former President Will Live With Stage 4 Cancer 'For The Rest Of His Life,' Has Slowed Down

He also thanked the doctors, nurses and other medical professionals who have treated him, saying their "skill, dedication, and compassion mean so much."

Biden used much of the message to urge men to discuss prostate cancer screening with their doctors, pointing to the dramatically higher survival rate when the disease is detected early.

Cancer Treatment Delays Surge Across Us As Doctor Warns System 'Needs Fixing Immediately'

"Talk to your doctors. Ask the hard questions. Do it for yourself, and do it for the people who love you," Biden wrote.

Biden said men at average risk should begin discussing prostate cancer screening with their doctors around age 50, while Black men and those with a family history should begin those conversations earlier.

Simple Sitting Change Linked To Lower Risk Of Cancer Death, Study Finds

The American Cancer Society recommends discussing screening at age 50 for average-risk men, age 45 for Black men and certain men with a family history, and age 40 for some men at even higher risk.

Biden's office announced in May 2025 that the former president had been diagnosed with an aggressive form of prostate cancer that had metastasized to his bones.

Joe Biden's Cancer Has Spread Further, Leaving Him In 'Very Painful' Condition, Hunter Reveals

The diagnosis came after Biden experienced increasing urinary symptoms and doctors discovered a prostate nodule. His office said at the time that the cancer had a Gleason score of 9, Grade Group 5, but was hormone-sensitive, allowing for effective management.

Biden later underwent radiation therapy and completed that course of treatment last fall.

Cancer Survivors Saw Major Improvements In Sleep And Well-being With One Weekly Practice

Fox News Digital reached out to Biden's office for additional comment on his current health, treatment and prognosis.

Biden closed Tuesday's message by thanking those who have continued to pray for him and his family.

"It's my hope and prayer that by sharing our experience and being part of this important conversation, we can help save lives," he wrote. "And no matter what, keep the faith. God bless you."

Fox News Digital's Stepheny Price and Robert McGreevy contributed to this reporting.

title: 2 women who killed transgender man Sam Nordquist get life sentences
description: Precious Arzuaga and Jennifer “Brooklyn” Quijano admitted to torturing and killing Sam Nordquist, a 24-year-old transgender man from Minnesota.
fullText:
A New York judge sentenced two women who admitted to torturing and murdering 24-year-old Sam Nordquist in 2025 to life in prison without the possibility of parole.

Precious Arzuaga and Jennifer "Brooklyn" Quijano both received the maximum sentence for their roles in Nordquist's death on Sept. 8, 2026.

Arzuaga, whom prosecutors have called the "ring leader" in the case, pleaded guilty to all 10 charges she faced in June, including first-degree murder, kidnapping, aggravated sexual assault, coercion and concealment of a human corpse. Quijano faced many of the same charges, including murder, kidnapping and conspiracy.

Prosecutors have said Arzuaga met Nordquist, a transgender man from Minnesota, on TikTok in the summer of 2024. The two began a romantic relationship, and Nordquist flew to the Canandaigua area of New York State to stay with Arzuaga for what his family believed was supposed to be a two-week vacation.

Arzuaga and Quijano admitted to torturing Nordquist to death between Jan. 1 and Feb. 1, 2025, along with five other defendants in room 22 of Patty's Lodge in Hopewell, New York, before disposing of his body in a field in Yates County.

"Sam came here looking for love, and sadly and tragically he found you," Ontario County Judge Kristina Karle told Arzuaga during her sentencing.

Linda Nordquist, Sam Nordquist's mother, provided her victim impact statement to the court during Arzuaga's sentencing Tuesday.

"Precious, you may have believed you had the power to decide how my son's story would end, but you did not," she said. She told the court that her son was kind, gentle, loving and trusting of others.

Ontario County First Assistant District Attorney James Nobles told the court that Arzuaga was at the center of the group accused of torturing Nordquist to death.

"I have no question in my mind that without her, Sam would be here today," Nobles told Judge Karle on Tuesday. He said her guilty plea saved the community and Sam's family from the depraved evidence and facts of the case, including a text she sent to her co-conspirators: "Sam can never leave New York alive."

Arzuaga then took her chance to speak, apologizing to Sam Nordquist's family.

"What was stated previously by the family was true. Sam really did love me and my kids, and I'm willing to accept whatever punishment you are to give me," Arzuaga said as people in the courtroom audibly laughed at her apology.

Judge Karle said Arzuaga's history of domestic incident reports with previous romantic partners showed a pattern of her behavior.

"When I was reading these reports, I was wondering why someone so good was taken tragically. Was it because Sam was everything you are not and would never be," Karle asked Arzuaga.

The courtroom filled with applause as Arzuaga was taken out of the courtroom.

Ontario County Assistant District Attorney Sara Van Strydonck told the court Tuesday that Quijano's motive in Nordquist's torture and killing was simple and common: jealousy.

Van Strydonck said Arzuaga and Quijano were once romantically involved, to the point where Quijano called Arzuaga her "baby moms" and Arzuaga called her "baby dads." Arzuaga, she said, was the one pulling the strings within the group, while Quijano was "the muscle behind it."

She explained that photo and video evidence in the case shows Quijano and the six other defendants pinning Nordquist between chairs in the corner of the room at Patty's Lodge while they berated him.

Nordquist was also forced into a dog cage on multiple occasions, and Quijano would refer to him as a "two-legged dog," Van Strydonck said.

Kayla Nordquist, Sam Nordquist's sister, gave her impact statement, telling Quijano that she continuously made choices that ultimately led to Sam's death.

"There are moments when I catch myself wondering if just one person had chosen differently, would my brother still be here," she said. "If one person said this is wrong. If one person helped him escape. If one person treated him as a human instead of an object that could be controlled."

Quijano's lawyer, Neil Gunther, told Judge Karle that Quijano was also a victim of Arzuaga. He explained that Arzuaga physically and mentally abused Quijano for years, and that Quijano takes responsibility for her actions.

"When I was in court last time, I could hear Sam's family crying, and I want them to know that I could feel that," Quijano said in a written statement her lawyers read aloud in court. "I'm sorry I hurt Sam, and I'm sorry I didn't help Sam."

Judge Karle said she appreciated what Gunther said and that it might have made sense that Quijano was also a victim of Arzuaga if she didn't participate in "these cruel, torturous, horrific, dehumanizing actions toward Sam."

She said Quijano could have been a savior to Nordquist, but instead she participated in his torture and enjoyed it.

"Calling a human being a two-legged dog and caging them," Judge Karle said with tears in her eyes. "That is not someone who is a bystander caught in the web of Precious Arzuaga."

Quijano and Arzuaga are the only two defendants who have been sentenced so far.

Emily Motyka and Kyle Sage have pleaded guilty to their roles in Nordquist's death. Sage's sentencing is scheduled for December, but Motyka's sentencing has not yet been scheduled.

Thomas Eaves, Kimberly Sochia and Patrick Goodwin are awaiting trial. Their trials are scheduled to start in January 2027.

Madison Scott is a New York Connect reporter, covering entertainment, breaking and consumer news, and trending topics with a focus on stories that matter to readers across New York State.

Contributing: Christopher Cann, USA TODAY

title: Scottish clubs face tougher Europa League route
description: Uefa have made changes to the qualifying rounds of the Europa League from next season.
fullText:
Uefa has made a change to the qualifying rounds of the Europa League which will make it more difficult for Scotland's representative to qualify for the league phase.

From next season, the final qualifying round will be split into paths for champions and non-champions, mirroring the system in the Champions League and the Conference League.

The Europa League third qualifying round currently has two paths, but condenses into one seeded draw of all teams in the final stage.

From next season, it will stay as two separate qualifying routes.

It means Scotland's representative will no longer be able to play the likes of Iberia 1999, Kairat Almaty or Ararat - three teams who dropped down from Champions League qualifying champions path.

Another season, another failure - where did it all go wrong for Celtic?

Rangers count consequences of European failure

The Scottish Cup winners - or if that team also wins the league title the Premiership runners-up - enter the Europa League in the first qualifying round next season.

The non-champions path is far stronger, as it includes teams who qualified by league placing from countries such as Belgium, Turkey, Czech Republic and Greece.

In addition, non-champions from the Champions League can drop into the path. This season, that was Olympiakos, Sparta Prague, Sturm Graz and Union St-Gilloise.

This season, Hearts were in the non-champions path and were eliminated by Benfica. Rangers, who were seeded, were knocked out at the same stage by Jagiellonia Bialystok.

With Celtic and Rangers' five-year coefficient falling due to poor performance by Scotland's clubs, they may well be unseeded next season, meaning a more difficult draw against one of the teams from a major league.

If the Scottish title winners drop out of Champions League and into the Europa League qualifying, they will play another team to drop down from the Champions League.

This season, Celtic entered the Champions League in the play-off round - meaning they were guaranteed to drop into the Europa League league phase.

But next season - due to Scotland dropping down the coefficient table - the champions will enter in the second qualifying round, and must win three ties to make it to the Champions League.

title: Remains found nearly 50 years ago identified as missing teenager
description: The teen, Cindy Marcell Blizzard, had run away in 1977, authorities said.
fullText:
Remains found nearly 50 years ago in North Carolina have been identified as those of a missing Maryland teenager, authorities announced, as investigators still seek answers on the cold case.

Skeletal remains and clothing were found in a wooded area in Wilson, North Carolina, in December 1977, according to the North Carolina State Bureau of Investigation. The remains, determined to have belonged to a female teenager or young woman, had likely been there for at least six months, it said.

Utah man's disappearance remains unsolved 17 years later

No match was found when comparing the dental records against missing persons cases, and the individual's identity remained unknown for decades due to limited forensic tools, the bureau said. The state reopened the case in 2010, but no match came back then, either, it said.

In 2024, the North Carolina State Bureau of Investigation's Cold Case Investigative Team assigned Special Investigator Andy Murr to review the case again, "this time with forensic tools that didn't exist in 1977," the bureau said in a press release on Tuesday.

Investigators were able to develop a DNA profile that could be used for forensic genetic genealogy. After submitting the profile to a genealogy service to find potential relatives, they were ultimately able to identify the remains as Cindy Marcell Blizzard, a 15-year-old girl who had run away from Monkton, Maryland, in the spring of 1977, the bureau said.

The FBI's National Crime Information Center, the Maryland Department of State Police Homicide Unit and the police department in Raleigh, North Carolina, helped confirm her identity, authorities said.

How a Colorado teen's unsolved disappearance baffles police a decade later

Following the initial discovery of the teen's remains, the state's chief medical examiner classified the manner of death as undetermined, though "circumstances surrounding the location and recovery of the remains raised the probability of foul play, and the investigators are treating the case as a homicide," the North Carolina State Bureau of Investigation said.

"Her death remains unsolved. Investigators are still looking for answers," the bureau said.

Anyone with information on the case is asked to call the North Carolina State Bureau of Investigation's cold case tip line at 919-582-TIPS, email coldcases@ncsbi.gov, or contact the Wilson County Sheriff's Office at 252-237-2118.
