title: Fantasy Football Week 1 Rankings: Hayden Winks' RB2 (Ranked 13-24) projections
description: Fantasy football analyst Hayden Winks reveals his RB2 rankings for Week 1.
fullText:
Fantasy football analyst Hayden Winks reveals his RB2 running back rankings and analysis for Week 1. He'll continue to update his rankings for every position throughout the week. He also wrote about his RB1 rankings for Week 1.

Alvin Kamara's status is unclear due to a training camp MCL injury, but that'd only change things on the margins. Etienne was paid well to be the base-down starter, a role that will lead to 15+ touches per week and almost all goal-line chances. In that role last year, Etienne was the per-game RB11 on RB14 usage.

The Saints' staff has talked up Etienne even more than the Jaguars ever did, and it's easy to argue this Saints OL will be the best he's played behind. It's an underrated good environment with New Orleans playing with the fastest neutral pace under HC Kellen Moore.

Join a Yahoo Fantasy Football league for the 2026 NFL season

The matchup is neutral at best. The Lions were the 12th-best defense against fantasy RBs last season and look a bit better up front this season, even if the secondary is worse. The Saints have the No. 21 projected team total (21.75) while playing on the road as 7.0-point dogs. Kamara missing would open up more reception chances, which could come in handy given the game script.

Etienne is projected for 12.8 half PPR points and 80.5 total yards by the betting markets. Those will go up if Kamara is ruled out. Audric Estimé and Kendre Miller were also dealing with injuries last week, and Devin Neal was released.

The Bills will make some changes to their offense with Joe Brady promoted to head coach and with the D.J. Moore addition. It's possible they are slightly more pass-heavy after being 26th in neutral pass rate since 2024 when Cook really broke out. Cook was only the RB39 in receptions per game last year, so he can't lose too many carries and still be the RB6 that he finished as last year. He'll likely catch an extra ball per game this year while having his rushing numbers dropping a bit. That's not a death sentence.

The matchup is that death sentence. The Texans have one of the best defenses on paper of the decade. They were the second-best defense against fantasy RBs last year after adjusting for schedule. Opposing RB rooms averaged 20 fewer rush yards per game against Houston compared to their season averages (third worst). Since then, they've added run-stopper Jadaveon Clowney and second-round NT Kayden McDonald to the rotation. Nasty work.

Cook's Week 1 projection is way lower than it typically is. He's only projected for 12.6 half PPR points on 93.5 total yards by the betting markets. His projected 74.5 rushing yards are almost exactly 20 yards less than last year's 94-yard average. That lines up with my data in the previous paragraph. Buffalo is only 23rd in projected points as 1.5-point road dogs, too.

This is the year to get excited for a top-15 season out of Hall. He's teased it many times, but the rest of the team wasn't ready. Geno Smith is a real upgrade over Justin Fields for the skill group, especially as this young Jets OL improved. That unit with star RT Armand Membou is approaching the very good tier. Even last year, Hall was the RB17, averaging 12.4 half PPR points in the 12 games without waived-QB Brady Cook.

The opening matchup in Tennessee is a little tougher than you'd think with HC Robert Saleh having star DT Jeffrey Simmons, DT John Franklin-Myers and EDGE Jermaine Johnson to work with. They should be better than the ninth-worse fantasy RB defense in 2026, though tackle-leading LB Cedric Gray is suddenly in the concussion protocol from an ATV accident.

The Jets are still only projected for 19.0 points here, the No. 29 projected team. Hall's bellcow status has him projected for 85.5 total yards and 12.9 half PPR points by the betting markets.

The Kyren versus Corum split will be a Week 1 takeaway on prime time, as the gap has slowly closed between the two over time. Williams played between 50% and 63% of the snaps over their final four games, including the playoffs. For comparison, Kyren's lowest snap rate in 2024 was 68%. In the final game of last year, they straight-up rotated drives:

The Rams were so prolific last year (29.9 points per game) that Kyren still finished as half PPR's RB8 on RB12 usage, despite Corum's explosive sidekick role. The Rams project for 26.0 points in Australia against the Niners, which is the fourth-most of the week.

San Francisco has injuries to note. Nick Bosa hasn't practiced much, but said, "I'm flying out there, I'm going to f--king play." Alrighty! He'll be joined by underrated star DT Osa Odighizuwa this year, with super star LB Fred Warner returning from injury. EDGE2 Mykel Williams (ACL) is out, though. With many of those players out last year, Williams posted 21.4 half PPR points on 84 total yards.

He projects for just 73.5 total yards and 11.6 half PPR points this time around as a clear RB2.

We'll learn more later in the week.

TreVeyon Henderson (ankle) hasn't practiced in weeks and has been ruled out for Week 1.

The Patriots averaged 19.6 half PPR points between the RB room, and Stevenson is set to inherit almost all of it with Corey Kiner as his backup. It's a low-end RB1 workload.

Unfortunately, it's a rematch of the Super Bowl loss, but now it's also in Seattle. The Seahawks were the best defense against fantasy RBs after adjusting for schedule; opposing RB rooms averaged 2.2 fewer points per game against them. They were first in stopping RB rushing TDs, though they did allow the most targets to RBs (7.1) at the same time. Stevenson should catch 3-4 passes here to provide some level of a floor. He scored 14.8 half PPR points on 63 total yards and five receptions in the Patriots' Super Bowl loss.

Stevenson has an 11.8-point projection in half PPR on 85.5 total yards by the betting markets. New England is 24th in projected points at 20.5. This will be a great test for a reworked interior OL that added injured star LG Alijah Vera-Tucker and moved 2025 third-round athlete Jared Wilson back to C.

Waiting on Sean Tucker's status after he missed practice on Tuesday. Irving lost the goal-line role to Tucker after returning from shoulder injury in Week 13 last year, so solidifying his goal-line role would be a big deal to his outlook, even with Kenny Gainwell projected to offload passing snaps.

Since entering the league, Irving is the per-game RB16 on RB20 usage in half PPR. His rookie season was electric with an elite play-caller and healthy OL, while last year's advanced numbers had Irving near the very bottom with the OL and himself injured. The Bucs OL could be the best in the NFL this year, and Irving has practiced for weeks coming off a shoulder surgery. There is certainly upside right out of the gate.

The Bengals will be better with star DT Dexter Lawrence and more experience at LB/S, but it's a great opening matchup regardless. Tampa Bay is 12th in projected points (23.5) in Cincy. Irving has 76.5 total yard and 11.2 half PPR points projection in the betting markets as a volatile RB2.

Skattebo came back from a dislocated ankle on time, didn't have a setback throughout training camp, and passed the eye test in preseason action. The Najee Harris signing is a potential long-term thorn, but that felt like an indictment on Tyrone Tracy Jr. and Devin Singletary more than one on their lead back.

Skattebo was the RB9 on RB15 usage when he went down with a Week 8 injury last year, catching 3.0 receptions per game and handling all of the goal line work. This version of the Giants will be more run committed with HC John Harbaugh bringing in Greg Roman types on the staff. All coaching and player quotes have suggested an extremely run-heavy approach with a FB and multiple TEs on the field. That's great for Skattebo.

The Giants were also 23rd in scoring during that eight-week sample with Skattebo, and they're projected for the No. 16 team total (22.75 points) this week while hosting the Cowboys. It helps that the Giants are adding Malik Nabers and first-round RG Francis Mauigoa to the offense.

Meanwhile, Dallas added star DT Quinnen Williams, first-round S Caleb Downs, first-round EDGE Malachi Lawrence, and others since Skattebo faced them, but he did hang 12.9 half PPR points on them in his starting debut last Week 2.

He's a quality low-end RB2. I like the higher on 10.2 half PPR points in the betting markets.

With Zach Charbonnet (ACL) out, Price enters the season as the clear-cut starter. He's expected to be the base-down back with George Holani in a passing down role. Holani is not a real threat to the goal-line role in ways that were annoying with the Kenneth Walker III and Charbonnet split. It's probably a better role for Price than what Walker had when he was the RB22 on RB27 usage while Charbonnet was healthy.

For reference, the Seahawks' entire RB room averaged 21.7 expected half PPR points from Week 1 through the Super Bowl last year, while whopping teams en route to 29.2 points per game (second most). It'll be very hard to replicate that consistent game script and explosive ability without OC Klint Kubiak.

The Patriots are a difficult matchup to open with, but they did at least lose run-stopping NT Kyhris Tonga this offseason. Last year's New England defense was fourth-best against fantasy RBs when adjusting for schedule. The Seahawks are projected for 24.0 points (11th), while Price has a wide range of outcomes on a projected 9.8 half PPR points per the betting markets.

Warren went overlooked in the offseason as an incumbent in an offense set up for players with his skill set. New HC Mike McCarthy typically likes passing more than running, and this version of Aaron Rodgers loves throwing to his RBs so he doesn't have to get hit or throw deep. Last year, the Steelers were fourth in RB usage because Kenny Gainwell was the RB4 in receptions per game (4.3). Warren caught 2.4 per game (RB19). I doubt Rico Dowdle touches either mark this year.

Warren should have FLEX value in a similar role to last year when he finished as the RB20 per game on RB21 usage. If he can keep some of the goal line role while absorbing more receptions, then he's going to beat ADP with ease. We'll learn more about the rotation after Week 1, but I'd be surprised if Warren isn't the starter.

The matchup is awesome. The Steelers are 13th in projected points while hosting the Falcons. They won't have either 2025 first-round edge this week, and the Falcons were league average against fantasy RBs last year with them. Assume the Falcons have a bottom-three DL right now and mediocre off-ball LBs.

Warren projects for 62.5 total yards and 9.6 half PPR points by the betting markets. Those are worse than he had last year for some reason. I disagree!

The Texans RB room averaged 16.0 half PPR points per game last year (28th), despite being 8th in carries. The OL was brutal, and they were also 27th in receptions. The hope is David Montgomery is much better than the recently-retired Nick Chubb and the new additions across the OL pay dividends. I'm skeptical.

Houston's OL still is an up-and-coming LT Aireontae Ersery, first-round rookie LG Keylan Rutledge, C Evan Brown ($2.4 million), RG Ed Ingram ($12.5M/year), and RT Trent Brown ($4.9M). That's an unproven left side and a contender for the worst right side in the NFL. Montgomery is a heady rusher, but he's also not explosive enough to create that much on his own in his age-29 season. Expect Woody Marks to rotate in both rushing and passing phases, even if Monty is the favorite for goal-line carries early on.

The Texans are 14th in projected points this week while hosting the Bills, who are unleashing a new 3-4 defense with DC Jim Leonard. Buffalo was the sixth-worst defense against fantasy RBs last year after adjusting for schedule. They played with a two-high shell at the third-highest rate last year, but more defenders in the box are expected this time around. It's a neutral to solid matchup on paper for Monty.

In the Panthers playoff game last year, Hubbard handled 17 touches and both goal-line touches with Rico Dowdle demoted to backup duties.

Jonathon Brooks has opposite traits to Dowdle as a better receiver and less proven short-yardage option. Brooks is also dealing with soreness, stemming from a twice-torn ACL. He's been working on the side with trainers. Meanwhile, Hubbard is fully healthy after an early-camp hamstring injury.

Hubbard is a clear favorite for the starting base-offense role in Week 1. This role led to an RB12 finish in half PPR points per game (on RB7 usage), back in 2024 for what it's worth. Project him for 15+ touches and the goal-line role initially. The Panthers are projected for the 21st-most points against the Bears this week. Chicago is one of the worst defenses on paper this year. This is probably the best week of the year for Hubbard. He's a FLEX starter.

title: How familiarity helped Jovaughn Gwyn win Ravens’ starting center job
description: Jovaughn Gwyn says his familiarity with Dwayne Ledford helped ease his move to Baltimore while also possibly helping him through competition.
fullText:
One of the biggest questions surrounding the Baltimore Ravens throughout training camp centered on the offensive line. More specifically, the center position. The story is well-known. The organization lost one of the game's best, and through seven rounds and 11 picks, they didn't select one during the NFL Draft.

Baltimore spent much of the summer evaluating options after offseason changes reshaped the interior of the line, creating one of the roster's most important competitions heading into Week 1. The battle ultimately ended with Jovaughn Gwyn earning the starting job (for Week 1 anyway).

Talent and performance were the primary factors, but Gwyn's comments this week suggested another element may have quietly helped his transition.

Familiarity between player and coach is at play here. Ravens Wire mentioned that, as an added benefit, he stacked solid showings. Before arriving in Baltimore, Gwyn spent time working under offensive line coach Dwayne Ledford while both were with the Atlanta Falcons.

When Ledford joined the Ravens staff, that previous relationship became relevant again. Gwyn explained that communication about a reunion was limited amid the uncertainty surrounding both men's futures. Once they arrived in Baltimore, however, the benefit of that prior experience became clear. Gwyn mentioned this in a recent interview with the Baltimore media.

"I kind of knew what [run game coordinator/offensive line coach Dwayne Ledford] would want in his offensive line, so just coming here, it was more — like I said — [about] just having [an] understanding of what he needed on a day-to-day basis from us, so it made it easier for me."

That may seem like a small detail, but it can be significant when players are learning a new scheme and competing for playing time. While other linemen were learning Ledford's expectations from scratch, Gwyn already understood many of the standards, coaching points, and daily demands of the system.

Gwyn repeatedly emphasized that earning the coaching staff's trust was one of his primary goals throughout camp. He described spending three seasons primarily in reserve roles while waiting for an opportunity to prove he could handle a starting assignment.

When that opportunity arrived, understanding exactly what his position coach expected may have helped accelerate the process. The familiarity also extended beyond scheme. Ledford already knew the type of player Gwyn was and what he brought to a locker room and meeting room. Gwyn, meanwhile, understood the level of accountability Ledford demanded from his offensive linemen.

That background alone wasn't enough to win the job. The Ravens still needed to see Gwyn perform, communicate effectively, and show he could handle one of the offense's most important positions. Still, familiarity can remove some of the uncertainty that comes with a coaching transition, and Gwyn's comments suggest he entered camp with a clearer understanding of what success looked like than most players learning a new system for the first time.

The decision now places one of Baltimore's biggest offseason questions squarely in Gwyn's hands. Replacing Tyler Linderbaum was never going to be about finding another Tyler Linderbaum. It was about finding a player the coaching staff trusted to direct protections, communicate across a rebuilt interior line, and help keep Lamar Jackson upright.

For at least Week 1, the Ravens believe they found that player. The next step is showing that the trust built through months of work — and a familiarity that began long before either man arrived in Baltimore — can hold up once the regular season begins.

This article originally appeared on Ravens Wire: How familiarity helped Jovaughn Gwyn win Ravens' starting center job

fullText:
Cameron Stanley talks up ‘revolutionary’ AI capabilities and says Washington working with Nato and Five Eyes partners

The Pentagon’s top artificial intelligence official said on Tuesday that America’s closest allies lack the resources to keep pace with the US military’s adoption of AI, and that Washington is working to steer them away from mistakes it made along the way.

“They don’t have the resources that we do, they don’t have the experience that we do, they don’t have the scale that we do,” Cameron Stanley, chief digital and artificial intelligence officer at the Department of Defense, said at an event at the Billington Cybersecurity summit. Of Nato and the Five Eyes, an intelligence-sharing partnership of the US, UK, Canada, Australia and New Zealand, Stanley said Washington was “actively working with a number of our partners” so “they don’t make the same mistakes that we make”.

The comments come less than a year into Stanley’s tenure, during which the Pentagon’s AI office has rolled out several new tools while losing a number of senior staff. Since January, Stanley has overseen the launch of GenAI.mil, an internal chatbot platform he says has reached 1.7 million users, and Agent Network, a system designed to shorten the time between intelligence-gathering and a commander’s decision. The defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, has directed Stanley’s office to report AI deployment speed as a monthly metric, part of a wider push to expand military computing power.

Much of Stanley’s appearance focused on speed. He described watching a commander halt a scheduled briefing to take a 30-second phone call and issue an order on the spot, without a formal decision brief or a review of the room’s security clearance level. He called the moment “revolutionary”.

“I know it sounds simplistic,” Stanley explained. “It’s only simplistic because we’re good at it now.”

It’s a term he has used before. Project Maven, the Pentagon’s original AI targeting program launched in 2017, became the Palantir-built Maven Smart System, which the US leaned on heavily during its 2026 air campaign against Iran, helping strike more than 13,000 targets over the first 38 days, according to Stanley at conference in May. Speaking at Palantir’s AIPCon 9 conference in March, Stanley called Maven “revolutionary” too, saying it let commanders go from identifying a target to launching a strike within a single platform.

But the campaign has drawn scrutiny. More than 120 members of the US Congress signed a letter demanding answers from the Pentagon regarding civilian casualties and the use of artificial intelligence, following a 28 February strike on an elementary school in Minab, which Iranian officials say killed at least 168 people, many of them children.

Stanley ended by telling the audience that the department’s old habits were now its biggest liability.

“The way we’ve always done it is the most risky course of action,” he said, adding that the department needed to “think differently” if it wants AI tools in the hands of warfighters faster.

fullText:
Once hailed as the future, even the likes of Google, Sony and Microsoft have struggled to make streaming games fun, fast or affordable

Don’t get Pushing Buttons delivered to your inbox? 
In August 2009, at the very first Gamescom expo, I sat in a small meeting room in Germany and played Mario Kart and World of Warcraft on a laptop, via technology that was then completely new: cloud gaming. It was a demonstration for a yet-to-be-launched service called Gaikai that promised to let you play any game in a browser window, without a console. (Here is an ancient video of that demonstration, featuring a very young Keza.) With a single click I could launch into any game, hosted on servers hundreds of miles away. It really did look like the future.

Since then, plenty of companies have tried to be the first to truly crack game streaming, vying to be the Netflix of games. Sony ended up buying Gaikai for $380m (£242m) in 2012; its technology now powers the streamable classic games library on PlayStation, and the PS5’s advanced game streaming. OnLive, Gaikai’s first competitor, launched in 2011 but shut down after less than a year, leaving Sony to acquire all its patents. Google’s Stadia cloud gaming service also imploded, launching in 2019 and shutting down three years later.

Despite the fact that people simply don’t seem to want game streaming services – or at least not enough to pay a stand-alone monthly subscription for them – Sony and Microsoft have remained steadfastly committed to the idea, bundling game streaming into their PlayStation Plus and Xbox Game Pass services. I use both quite regularly when I want to check out a game quickly, mostly because modern download sizes are ridiculous (Final Fantasy VII Rebirth, say, takes up nearly 150GB of my PS5 space, almost a quarter of its usable storage). Who wants to do 30 minutes of hard drive management every time they want to play something new?

Last week, however, Microsoft announced that it was introducing time limits for game streaming: you’re now allowed 5-15 hours a month, depending on your subscription tier. And yes, you’re right: that is not enough time to play through even one single average-sized game. This brings Microsoft’s previously unwavering commitment to cloud gaming into question – and when even Microsoft with its infinite resources can’t seem to make it work, is the writing on the wall for game streaming as a whole?

In the early days, the biggest problem with streaming was input lag: the time it took for the game to respond to your button-pressing. Normally, when you’re playing a game this lag is imperceptible. Via streaming, it would often be horribly obvious, your character taking maybe a full second to jump after you’d pressed the A button. Not all games rely heavily on timing and finesse, but a lot of them do, and playing games on a minor time-delay felt nauseating.

This is much less of an issue now, but another problem has only gotten worse: game streaming requires the instantaneous transmission of a lot of data, making it taxing on your internet connection and expensive for the service provider. Here’s a comparison: watching an hour of Netflix uses about 1GB of data. An hour of game streaming via Xbox requires about 4GB. Microsoft’s servers have to stream you the video of your live gameplay, and continually receive and interpret your controller inputs. No wonder Microsoft suddenly wants to limit your hours.

The cloud gaming model has always been based on the idea that data infrastructure would become faster and cheaper in the future. Its selling point is outsourcing computing power so that you can play whatever you want without upgrading your console or PC, or even without having one at all. Unfortunately, thanks to AI companies and their chatbots’ bottomless demand for computing power and energy, the opposite has happened. Data and computing power are now more expensive. Ironically, this change has been driven by Microsoft itself as much as anything else: a huge chunk of the company’s spending went on data centres and AI infrastructure in the last fiscal year. This suggests that Microsoft is choosing to prioritise data provision for users of Azure and Copilot over its gaming customers.

Will this affect you? Probably not. Only 4% of all Game Pass subscribers use it for more than 15 hours a month, Microsoft said in a blog post announcing the changes. Which brings us right back to the question: if cloud gaming really is the future, why is nobody using it? It’s been a long time since that 2009 demo, and this technology has still yet to meaningfully break through. Is it time to give up on it?

Alongside Sony and Microsoft, there is one other player left in this death match: the US-based tech firm Nvidia, whose GeForce Now game-streaming service (launched in 2013 and revamped many times since) might just be the world’s most successful. Nvidia has been riding high on the AI boom, becoming the most valuable company in the world. Its computing hardware powers all the datacentres that the rest of the tech industry has been building, to satisfy imagined future AI demand. Perhaps, when all of this shakes out, it will be the only company left that can afford to provide game streaming services at all.

I have been variably unwell for most of the summer, and in need of something absorbing, so I dived into Kingdom Come Deliverance II – think Skyrim, but 15th-century historical fiction.

I was impressed immediately by the outstanding script, story and performances, all of which are much more humorous and entertaining than I was expecting from a hardcore medieval RPG. And I also love how unashamedly laborious this game is: you must control each swipe of a drawn-out sword fight; you have to manually grind and mix herbs for health-restoring concoctions; and if you want anyone to speak to you, you must regularly wash your face (and grubby tunic) so you don’t stink. Last night, I spent 20 minutes hammering out horseshoes in the forge. The opening hours have you hauling sacks of flour around while a tavern landlady swears at you.

I can’t help but respect this naturalist commitment to grime and busywork; knight-life isn’t all horseplay, you know. I have spent many, many hours with this game and I am still basically a stinking peasant. I may well never finish it, but I am resolved to at least get to the point where I have my own steed and a pair of decent boots.

Available on: Xbox, PlayStation 5, PC

 Estimated playtime: 55+ hours

A Nintendo broadcast on Tuesday spilled a bunch of new details about the upcoming Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake, which I’m relieved to say is looking beautiful. Link looks doll-like in the updated style, and Hyrule Castle Town looks a bit like a living Playmobil village overlaid with a watercolour-ish filter that makes the whole game look like something half remembered. (I am somewhat less enthused by the addition of voice acting to the cutscenes; Navi was already annoying enough.) Check out the demo here.

For the Ringer, frequent Guardian games contributor Lewis Gordon has written this excellent long-read on Japanese publisher Capcom’s current streak of brilliance, talking to a host of executives and developers about exactly how the company has bucked the trend while the rest of the games industry is on fire.

Patrick Miller – better known as pattheflip – has published a thought-provoking reflection on how and why some players become overinvested – even dependent – on video games. “I say this as someone who has loved video games his whole life; if games serve a load-bearing function in someone’s life, it’s the life that needs fixing, not the games.”

At the end of last week, the White House released this horrible little propaganda arcade, featuring nasty riffs on popular games, such as a version of Tetris where you have to build a wall on the Mexican border to stave off “the coming horde”. That particular game was later removed after The Tetris Company expressed its opposition.

Grand Theft Auto VI: can playing a video game count as cheating on your partner?

Thieves target mail order sales as Pokémon card prices soar

‘Ruin and decay bring a chance of rebirth’: Hidetaka Miyazaki on uniting players in a damaged world

Reader Piero sent in this question (along with some super-nice feedback on the newsletter – thank you, Piero!):

“I enjoy the occasional foray into story-driven RPGs, such as Kingdom Come Deliverance, Skyrim and the Baldur’s Gate series, but as I get older I’m finding the continual combat sections overwhelming and dull. Could you recommend me some good RPGs that don’t rely on combat as the main game mechanic?”

You’re not alone, Piero – for a surprising proportion of players, combat is just something you have to do in order to get to the bits of a game that you find more interesting. Most RPGs these days have a “story mode” option that at least makes all the fighting trivially easy, if you’re not interested in engaging with it. There is of course Disco Elysium, a complex role-playing game with no combat at all; like Citizen Sleeper, it is mostly text-based. I have heard good things about Eastshade, an open-world game where you’re a painter rather than a fighter. I’d also suggest Pentiment, though it’s a very different style from Skyrim. And Yonder: The Cloud Catcher Chronicles is worth a look if you don’t mind cutesy.

If you have a question for Question Block – or anything else to say about the newsletter – hit reply or email us at pushingbuttons@theguardian.com.

title: OpenAI Just Launched ChatGPT Images 2.5, and Here’s How It Compares to Google’s Nano Banana 2
description: OpenAI has pushed out ChatGPT Images 2.5, which it describes as faster, sharper, and smarter. How does it compare to Gemini's best?
fullText:
In among the maelstrom of everything else that's happening with AI right now, OpenAI has pushed out ChatGPT Images 2.5, which it describes as faster, sharper, and smarter, with "better tools for creating whatever you can dream of." Those new tools include templates, more precise editing features, and a way of converting your on-screen doodles into fully realized images.

Does all of this mean ChatGPT Images 2.5 will save us from the scourge of bad AI food images on menus and posters? Can it replace a traditional photo editor? And how does it compare to the impressive Nano Banana 2 update that Google pushed out in February?

To answer all these questions and more, I fired up the new image generator in ChatGPT to see what it was capable of. Everyone is getting it—it's rolling out for all users across the web, the desktop apps, and the mobile apps now—though as usual there are varying usage limits (which ChatGPT only vaguely defines) on each plan.

The sameness and uncanny look of AI-generated food on restaurant signs and menus is becoming a real issue, so this seemed like a good place to start. It's fair to say that promotional images of food have always taken some artistic license, but AI is making the problem worse. Can ChatGPT Images 2.5 help?

Here's what I tried: "Create a 1:1 aspect ratio image with four squares inside it for a fast food restaurant display. The images should show (from top to bottom, left to right) a cheeseburger, six nuggets, a box of fries, and a Coke. Make the pictures look as photorealistic as possible with natural lighting, but add variations and imperfections to give the impression of real food."

ChatGPT is on the left and Gemini on the right. Both do a decent job of producing menu items that look realistic and actually edible, albeit with the usual AI tendency towards the generic. Personally, I'd say the ChatGPT images look slightly more like real food, though Gemini has done better on the backgrounds and wider scene (the Burger King logo would cause trouble, though).

One of the key new features in ChatGPT Images 2.5 is a new Sketch tool, which lets you turn your basic scribblings into full pictures. Click or tap the + (plus) button in the prompt box to find it—if you're on mobile you'll also have to choose Plugins from the sub-menu that pops up.

The tool lets you play around with colors, shapes, and text, and when you're done you can add a text prompt to it—something like "turn this sketch into the sort of illustration you might see in a high-quality children's book, complete with stars and distant planets" (which is the prompt I used here).

Gemini doesn't have a Sketch tool per se, though it's easy enough to add an image to a prompt for inspiration. Google's AI went far more traditional with its illustration and decided to drop in an alien astronaut, whereas ChatGPT used a touch more realism. Both do the job well enough, but if I had to pick, I think I'd take the Gemini one.

OpenAI is talking up the improved precision in editing with ChatGPT Images 2.5, so I gave it a go after submitting the following prompt: "Create a photorealistic picture of a cabin sat deep in the woods, in its own clearing, with trees all around. It's early morning and the sun shines through the foliage, while the cabin itself looks modern and welcoming."

Click on a ChatGPT image and you can add comments about specific aspects of the image, mark up sections of the picture to change, and quickly erase parts of it or the entire background. I tried getting it to remove some cabin furniture and change the time of day from early morning to dusk, and it completed the brief with aplomb—with the rearranged shadows a particularly clever touch.

Gemini gives you a simpler set of editing tools when you click on an image, but the basics are the same: Use text comments or scribbled annotations to specify the changes. Again, I got the AI to remove some cabin chairs (there must be a lot of chairs in AI model training data), and switch the scene to dusk. Gemini did fine as well, but ultimately the ChatGPT effort looked a little more lived-in and a little less artificial.

These two AI bots are very close in performance when it comes to image generation. Gemini is no slouch, and Nano Banana 2 is excellent at almost everything, but I think ChatGPT Images 2.5 has a slight edge at the moment—particularly if you add in the extra features for sketching and saving prompts as templates.

The debate over when and why to use these tools continues, and I think there will always be more value in actual human art and photography, no matter how good AI gets at making pictures. A real forest is always going to beat an approximation of one stitched together by AI. For visualizations and ideas where you wouldn't employ an artist or have the design chops to do it yourself, though, both Gemini and ChatGPT are at a higher level than ever.

It's the editing tools that are potentially the most useful at this point: Changes to pictures that would usually take professionals hours can now be done by anyone, in seconds, and the capabilities are only going to improve in the future.

title: GAA refute misogyny in 'strongest possible terms'
description: GAA director general Tom Ryan says the organisation's commitment to integration remains "firm and absolute" in the wake of comments made by former Irish president Dr Mary McAleese.
fullText:
GAA director general Tom Ryan has said the organisation's commitment to integration remains "firm and absolute" in the wake of comments made by former Irish president Dr Mary McAleese.

In February 2024, the Gaelic Athletic Association [GAA], Ladies Gaelic Football Association [LGFA] and the Camogie Association announced an intention to merge into one body.

Dr McAleese resigned from her position as chair of the committee tasked with overseeing the amalgamation on Tuesday and said she was "devastated" that the stated target of 2027 would not he met. She added she was "dubious" of the GAA's commitment to integration.

Ryan told RTE Radio's Morning Ireland, external that he "can't accept" the idea that the missed target is a result of misogyny.

"I would refute that in the strongest possible terms," he said.

"I accept in the course of a project like this there will be different perspectives, and different points of view and that's fine but I can't accept that as a charge.

"I'm very, very proud to be part of the GAA. I'm proud of what it is and does.

"It's an inclusive organisation, it's a family-orientated organisation, it's a progressive organisation, and in leadership terms both nationally and locally, there are countless women who play a huge part in guiding and driving the organisation."

'GAA integration target will be very hard to meet'

Begley calls for 'positivity' on Gaelic games merger

Ryan said the original target of 2027 had proven to be "a little bit too ambitious" but that integration will still happen through a "phased implementation".

He added: "I don't see a future for us as a standalone organisation, promoting and offering male sports only. Our future is together.

"We will be far stronger as a combined organisation. I believe that. The GAA believes that. I know my colleagues in ladies football and camogie believe that.

"All we are looking at here is we've missed a deadline, our own deadline. Our job now is to just recast things in light of that, to learn from that and push ahead."

title: Williams will command respect as Wales coach - Vokes
description: Sam Vokes believes Ashley Williams will "command respect" as part of Craig Bellamy's Wales staff, despite his lack of coaching experience.
fullText:
Former Wales striker Sam Vokes believes Ashley Williams will "command respect" as part of Craig Bellamy's backroom staff despite his lack of coaching experience.

Williams, who has primarily worked as a pundit since retiring in 2021, joined the Wales coaching staff as an assistant on Monday along with former Swansea boss Alan Sheehan.

It will be the 42-year-old Uefa A Licence holder's first senior coaching job and comes after Piet Cramers and James Rowberry exited the Wales set-up.

Vokes, a member of the Wales squad that reached the Euro 2016 semi-final with Williams as captain, feels his former team-mate will be an asset.

"I was a bit shocked because I'd seen the success Ash has had in the media world - you see him on a Saturday night if you turn on Match of the Day," Vokes told BBC Radio Wales.

"It's a good recruitment by Bellamy because I played underneath Ash as a captain, and he was a great leader in the dressing room and led by example in the way he conducted himself on and off the pitch.

"He can be someone who speaks from experience and [will] go into that dressing room and immediately command respect.

"It will be great for the younger lads who have seen him play over the years. He'll bring all the experience he's got into that set-up.

"The first camp - away at Portugal and Denmark in the top end of the Nations League - he has played in those environments.

"He will be able to speak to the lads that are going out in those environments because he led by example, and led in the trenches many times."

Williams completed his coaching badges under the Football Association of Wales' umbrella alongside Vokes, and will get his first taste in the dugout with a trip to Portugal on Thursday, September 24.

That will be the first of four Nations League fixtures as part of an extended international break that also includes a double-header against Denmark and a home game against Norway.

Vokes believes the new set-up will favour Bellamy, who was in talks to take the Burnley job in August, as the Wales head coach will be afforded more training time.

"I remember going into international camps, and you'd only be away for two or three days when you had to prepare for a game," Vokes recalled.

"Sometimes you are away for 10 days and have got to squeeze two games into that, which is a lot of work.

"The way Craig Bellamy works, he likes to get his players regimented and back on side with playing the way he likes.

"This three-week gap is a good opportunity for him to get them in for a good amount of time and work on that, but they are going to be tough games."

Bellamy is scheduled to announce his squad on Tuesday, 15 September.

title: 'Spoke brilliantly' but Liverpool fans torn on Mac Allister contract comments
description: Alexis Mac Allister splits opinion on his public comments regarding his contract at Liverpool, as fans and BBC Sport pundit Pat Nevin share opinions.
fullText:
Did Alexis Mac Allister strike the right tone when he told the media about his contract situation with Liverpool?

The Argentine midfielder has a deal with the Reds until 2028, but said on Tuesday that he is "very sad" not to have received a new contract in the summer after team-mates Dominik Szoboszlai and Ryan Gravenberch penned new agreements.

The public approach to stalling contract dealings is nothing new at Liverpool.

In November 2024, Mohamed Salah spoke openly about his contract stalemate when he admitted he was "disappointed" by a lack of offers from the club, as he entered the final six months of his deal.

Salah was eventually offered an extension and Mac Allister will be hoping for the same.

But as they were with Salah, opinions are split on whether taking it public was the fair thing to do.

Fans contacting BBC Sport claim the ordeal is "self-indulgent", while former Everton and Chelsea winger, Pat Nevin believes Mac Allister "said exactly the right things".

Nevin told BBC Radio 5 Live's Football Daily podcast: "I often hear various players saying things and pushing things a certain way and you get a bit fed up with it.

"You're thinking, 'go whinge and whine somewhere else mate, you're doing OK'. Not this time.

"I thought he spoke brilliantly. I thought he said exactly the right things - that he loves the club. Any fan watching that is thinking how he just wants to play for Liverpool Football Club.

"He's just shown us that is the case and if you are asked the question you answer it honestly. He is saying he's seen his mates getting these contracts which might be disappointing, but he's saying all the correct things I think.

"I take nothing away from that, I applaud him for all that.

"Things can change very quickly. It didn't look like Cody Gakpo would leave very recently and then suddenly he's knocking.

"If he is asking for far too much money and putting that pressure on it then he is playing a very good game because to speak the way he did there didn't sound like that. It sounded like somebody who just wanted a contract offered."

BBC Radio Merseyside also discussed the situation with Liverpool fan, Joel Richards, who called Mac Allister's comments a "clever tactic".

"Mac Allister's at an age now, 27, where his next contract is going to be the biggest one of his career," Richards said.

"He is someone who will be looking to be remunerated properly after seeing his team-mates getting bumper pay rises so, of course he's going to put it out there that he came very close to leaving in the summer.

"I'd say it's a clever tactic but how many times have we been here with footballers when they get a microphone put in front of them? If it wasn't going to happen here before a Champions League game, it would have happened with Argentina on international duty.

"Objectively speaking, if you're going to canvas the opinions of a decent size of Liverpool fans from last season, asked them what you thought on Mac Allister and whether he was deserving of a new deal, I think a large majority of that sample size would say 'no' simply because of the performances that he put in.

"However, it's easy to focus on the negatives of last season whereas, his first two seasons at Liverpool he was an important player for us."

Liverpool's communications department have dealt with tricky player-led controversies in recent times.

Salah told media he had been "thrown under the bus" during a stand-off with former boss Arne Slot last season, Dominik Szoboszlai had to clear up a move to shrug his shoulders at fans after defeat at Manchester City and now Mac Allister has made contract frustration public.

Some fans think the World Cup winner could have held back.

Writing in to BBC Sport, supporter Rob said Mac Allister "should do his talking on the pitch, not off it", while fan Patricio said the move was "childish" and that the midfielder should "earn" an extension.

BBC Sport reader David wrote: "Very poor from Mac Allister on so many levels. He still has two years remaining on his existing contract, had a very poor season so is not in a position to renegotiate terms unlike other players he referred to, and no doubt he is fully aware there will be a time to negotiate a new contract later in the season if his form improves."

And fan Stuart added: "Self-indulgent and not in any way helpful. Alexis was there to represent the club ahead of a huge match and first major Anfield occasion for Iraola, not to air his contract grievance. You're not bigger than the club even if you are a World Cup winner."

Mac Allister 'sad' at no Liverpool contract offer

title: Ukraine federation calls for Russian sanctions by FIA
description: Ukraine's national motorsport authority calls on FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem to impose sanctions on its Russian counterpart for opening offices in occupied parts of Ukraine.
fullText:
Ukraine's national motorsport authority has called on FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem to impose sanctions on its Russian counterpart.

The Russian automobile federation has opened offices in occupied parts of Ukraine in violation of the rules of the FIA, motorsport's governing body, according to the Ukraine federation (FAU).

The offices in Crimea, the city of Sevastopol and the Donetsk and Zaporizhzhia Oblasts are all located in areas recognised as sovereign Ukrainian territory by the United Nations.

The FAU's appeal for sanctions against its Russian counterpart (RAF) is the latest step it has made following the FIA's decision last month to lift the ban on Russian and Belarusian competitors in motorsport.

The FAU said in a statement that it was "outraged by the prolonged inaction of the global governing body".

It added: "The FAU has already appealed to the FIA senate and FIA ethics committee, but has received no reaction or reply."

It has also lodged a case with the FIA's international court of appeal.

FAU president Oleksander Feldman has written to Ben Sulayem demanding action.

He wrote: "Such short-sighted and counterproductive inaction is unbecoming of representatives of a global governing body. The current situation could have catastrophic consequences for the FIA's global standing.

"This is a dangerous precedent that paves the way for member organisations to disregard other provisions of the statutes and requirements of the rules, potentially leading to chaos and jeopardising the FIA's future as an institution."

Ukraine escalates protest over FIA lifting Russia ban

The FIA's rules permit only one automobile club or national sporting authority per country.

Feldman's letter demands that Ben Sulayem suspends Russia's membership, re-imposes "strict restrictions on Russian athletes' participation in international competitions", and makes a statement that publicly declares, on behalf of the FIA, that "the forcible redistribution of sporting authority is unacceptable".

The letter comes a week after Ukraine's minister for youth and sport told BBC Sport the FIA was wrong to lift the ban on Russian competitors.

Matvii Bidnyi said: "The reasons why Russia was banned from international sports competition have not disappeared. Nothing changes and it became even worse."

"Russia continues full-scale aggression against Ukraine. Belarus continues to provide military support to Russia. Ukrainian people are still being killed every day. And Russian attacks become more and more brutal.

"I don't understand, and Ukrainian people and I know that all European people don't understand what's happened, why now we must make this policy softer."

The ban on Russian and Belarusian competitors taking part in international motorsport events was imposed in February 2022, after Vladimir Putin ordered the invasion of Ukraine.

It was lifted on 3 August in a decision by the FIA's world motorsport council. This followed the International Olympic Committee, with which the FIA is affiliated, lifting its own ban.

Other sporting authorities, such as World Athletics, have not followed suit.

The Russian Embassy in London said in a statement to BBC Sport last week: "Excluding Russian athletes from international competitions amounts to segregation based on nationality and is incompatible with the principles of the Olympic charter.

"The FIA's decision to lift the restrictions on Russian competitors in international motorsport is a step in the right direction. It shows that common sense is gradually prevailing over political bias in major sporting federations."

The FIA has been contacted for comment.

Listen to Back at Base on BBC Sounds

title: Irvine stays as Pocognoli refreshes Scotland staff
description: Everton assistant Alan Irvine will continue as part of a refreshed Scotland coaching staff under new boss Sebastien Pocognoli.
fullText:
Everton assistant Alan Irvine will continue as part of a refreshed Scotland coaching staff under new boss Sebastien Pocognoli.

The former West Brom manager, who signed Belgian Pocognoli as a player during his brief stint at The Hawthorns in 2014, joined Steve Clarke's national team set-up after Euro 2024.

Pocognoli was appointed Clarke's successor last month and the Scottish FA have confirmed Irvine will be joined by two new faces, as well as goalkeeping coach Chris Woods, who was part of the previous regime.

Former Belgium coach Luke Benstead and Cameron Campbell, who worked in both Aberdeen and Rangers' academies before joining RB Leipzig in 2024 as their head of player development, have also been appointed as assistants to Pocognoli.

Campbell, 35, became Tottenham Hotspur's first-team individual development coach last year, while former Everton and Manchester United analyst Benstead was appointed Istanbul Basaksehir's assistant manager 12 months ago.

With Pocognoli's backroom team now in place, the former Monaco and Union St-Gilloise boss will name his first Scotland squad on Tuesday before his maiden camp.

Two Nations League fixtures against Slovenia come either side of encounters with Switzerland and North Macedonia during an extended international period.

"It was important for me to assemble the right backroom staff at the start of this new challenge," said Pocognoli. "I took my time and did my research, and I'm delighted with the group we have.

"I am really pleased that Alan didn't hesitate in agreeing to stay on. His passion for the role is obvious, as is his quality on the training pitch. He has the respect of everyone who has worked with him.

"I was very impressed by Cameron Campbell when I met him, and the recommendations I have received on him from trusted contacts in the English Premier League and in Germany, has been outstanding. It is a bonus that Cameron is Scottish.

"Luke was known to me from his time in Belgium, where he has worked with some big talents in his seven years with the national team. He has such a rounded skillset, having worked as a performance analyst then as an assistant coach at the highest level, with that added responsibility for set-pieces, which he will continue with Scotland. His enthusiasm to join this exciting project really stood out.

"The same applies to Chris Woods. Not only on the back of a standout playing career, where he played international football, but for his expertise as a goalkeeping coach working with some excellent goalkeepers."

title: Australian Poulton appointed England women's chief
description: The England and Wales Cricket Board appoints Australian Leah Poulton as the managing director of England women.
fullText:
The England and Wales Cricket Board has appointed Australian Leah Poulton as the managing director of England women.

The 42-year-old former batter, who played 90 times for her country, will start in November, succeeding Clare Connor.

Poulton has previously been the assistant coach of Sydney Thunder and Sydney Sixers in the Women's Big Bash League and was at Cricket New South Wales (NSW) as pathway manager and assistant coach for NSW Breakers.

She had a spell as high performance coach at Cricket Australia before becoming head of elite female cricket at Cricket NSW in a position she has held for the past six years.

The ECB said Poulton would be "accountable for the performances of England women, England women A, England women U19s and the overall effectiveness and reputation of the women's high-performance system".

It added: "Working closely with England women's head coach Charlotte Edwards and captain Nat Sciver-Brunt, she will set a clear, unified vision for England women to consistently succeed on the world stage."

England will host Australia in a women's Ashes next summer.

"I'm incredibly excited and honoured to be joining England and to have the opportunity to help shape our programmes and, most importantly, invest in our people," said Poulton.

"I'm looking forward to working with Charlotte, Nat and the wider team, building on the strong foundations already in place and taking the programme forward.

"I know how vital strong pathways and a healthy domestic game are to sustained success, so I'm looking forward to connecting with people across the game and helping give the next generation of English players every opportunity to thrive. It's a huge privilege to be part of England women and I can't wait to get started."

Once again, English cricket looks to the antipodes for a leader. The England men's team has two head coaches from New Zealand - Stephen Fleming and Brendon McCullum - and a selector from Australia in Marcus North.

Now in Leah Poulton, another Australian goes in at the top of the game in this country. The appointment is part of significant changes in the set-up of the England women's team.

Along with Clare Connor, women's performance manager Jonathan Finch has also left the ECB and Poulton effectively comes in as a replacement for both.

In her time at the ECB, Connor had many different roles, acting as deputy chief executive of the organisation as well as holding positions at the International Cricket Council and Marylebone Cricket Club.

Poulton will have a much clearer focus, concentrating on everything to do with the senior women's team and the pathways that lead to it. For that reason, she is likely to be more hands-on than Connor.

She is thought to have beaten some significant figures in the English game to land the job and has previously worked with head coach Charlotte Edwards and selector Lydia Greenway in the Big Bash. Poulton is known as a calm, clear communicator, not afraid to have difficult conversations when required.

Poulton arrives at a rare time of calm for the senior women's team, who are next in action after Christmas. The focus in the early part of the winter will be on the squads below the elite level.

But the new year is as big as it gets for English cricket, with attention turning to an home Ashes series in the summer - and it will be an Aussie in charge of finally regaining the urn.

title: 'This Is Anfield' sign fetches £115k at auction
description: The original sign from Liverpool's stadium tunnel fetched almost eight times its estimated guide price.
fullText:
The original "This Is Anfield" sign from Liverpool's stadium tunnel has fetched £115,000 under the hammer.

It sold for almost eight times the estimated guide price of £15,000, auctioneer Budds said.

The words famously hang above the passage to the pitch and Reds players traditionally touch the sign before matches as they pass. Legendary manager Bill Shankly chose them in 1972 after rejecting "Welcome To Anfield" as too friendly.

The original sign was removed in the 1970s and given to Ronald Wilson, a former member of the club's boys' team, whose family displayed it in an Isle of Man hotel for more than 20 years - until now.

Budds said famous players including Alan Hansen, Kenny Dalglish and Frank McGarvey had been pictured with the sign after joining Liverpool between 1977 and 1979.

The feature remained at Anfield during Liverpool's first two European Cup victories, in 1977 and 1978.

Budds said a groundsman proposed the original idea for the sign to club secretary Peter Robinson before Shankly suggested the amendment to "This Is Anfield".

Shankly said the sign was intended to remind Liverpool players who they represented while acting as a form of intimidation for visiting teams as they walked out into the ground.

Former Reds player George Scott said Shankly wanted any opposition player passing beneath the sign to know they were "going into a cauldron and they weren't going to come out with a win".

The auction house said former player Roy Evans, who managed the club between 1994 and 1998, gave the sign to Wilson.

It was displayed in Wilson's family's Rutland Hotel in Douglas from 1979 until 2000 before passing to his children.

The sign was later displayed in his son's office until his retirement in early 2026.

The identity of the new owner of the sign is not known.

title: The Rwandan eyeing Champions League history against Man Utd
description: Rwanda forward Joy-Lance Mickels has helped Azerbaijan's Sabah reach the Champions League proper on their competition debut, and is now looking to down the team he supports.
fullText:
Joy-Lance Mickels has been a Manchester United fan since childhood, and on Thursday the Rwanda international will fulfil a lifelong dream.

The 32-year-old is expected to start up front when Azerbaijani side Sabah travel to the home of the Red Devils in the opening round of the league phase of this year's Champions League (20:00 BST).

"I watch every [Man Utd] game when I can," he told the BBC World Service.

"It was the best draw we [Sabah] got in my opinion. It makes it even better because we're going to play in Old Trafford.

"Manchester United are one of the biggest clubs in the world so it will be a proud moment to step out on to the pitch."

Mickels is in his second stint with the side based in the town of Masazir, which lies about 16km (10 miles) north-west of the capital Baku.

He has played an important role in helping the Azerbaijan Premier League champions progress this far on their debut in the competition.

The forward scored four times in qualifying as the club, founded just nine years ago, navigated four two-legged ties to reach the Champions League proper.

One of those goals was the strike which ultimately sealed a 6-4 aggregate win over Israeli side Hapoel Be'er Sheva after a 94th-minute goal had forced the play-off tie into extra time.

"Reaching the Champions League is an historic achievement for Sabah and starting the league phase at Old Trafford makes it even more exciting," Mickels said.

"At the same time, we're not going there only to enjoy the atmosphere. We want to compete to represent not only our club but Azerbaijan in the best possible way and show we deserve to be there."

Mickels spent the first half of his career in the lower leagues in Germany, where he was born and raised, but has also had stints in the Netherlands and Saudi Arabia.

His first spell with Sabah came between 2021 and 2023, and he returned to the Bank Respublika Arena two years ago.

"My career has not always followed a straight or easy path," he explained.

"I have played at different levels and in several countries. But every experience has helped me grow both as a footballer and as a person."

He qualifies to represent Rwanda through his parents and made his international debut for the Wasps in March.

Mickels is now set to be the first footballer from the East African nation to play in the Champions League proper.

"I'm very proud of my Rwandan roots," he said.

"Representing Rwanda whilst playing the Champions League is very, very special.

"I hope my journey can help inspire young Rwandan players and show them that with belief, hard work and patience, it is possible to reach the pinnacle of football."

Champions League returns - who are favourites and players to watch?

Bouaddi impresses on first start - have Man City found 'a gem'?

After beginning their Champions League campaign at Old Trafford, Sabah's fixture list is littered with glamourous ties including home games against former champions Borussia Dortmund and Barcelona.

Yet, with their ground not meeting Uefa regulations, they are expected to stage those matches at the Olympic Stadium in Baku.

The Owls have another trip to England in their final fixture, when they face reigning Premier League champions Arsenal.

"Every match in the Champions League is special because you are competing against some of the best teams and players in Europe," Mickels said.

"Of course, Manchester United and Barcelona immediately stood out because of their history and global reputation.

"Playing at Old Trafford and welcoming Barcelona to Baku are the kinds of occasions every footballer dreams about. But we should respect every opponent and each match will be an opportunity for us to test ourselves at the highest level."

Mickels scored 19 goals as Sabah won a maiden league title last season, but he knows they will be underdogs in their Champions League outings.

However, he sees reaching the league phase as "a historic opportunity".

"We want to be competitive in every match and demonstrate the qualities that brought us this far," he added.

"We know that the level will be extremely high, but we believe in ourselves and the strength of our team. We want to gain valuable experience, create memorable moments for our supporters and earn as many points as possible."

Sabah's manager Valdas Dambrauskas has his own remarkable story, having used his winnings from an appearance on the Lithuanian version of Who Wants to Be a Millionaire? to forge a career in the game.

Mickels admits that while featuring in the Champions League proper is "a special feeling" for everyone at the club, the squad still fully intend to make an impact.

"We want to make the most of it whilst enjoying the challenge and continuing to grow as a team.

"We want to go out with some points and we're going to make it difficult for everybody to get points on us. This is the target."

title: Real Madrid? Ajax? Liverpool? Ranking Europe's greatest football dynasties
description: Paris St-Germain are eyeing a third successive Champions League crown, but where do they rank against Europe's most dominant clubs?
fullText:
Some find success sweet but fleeting, others spend years building to the pinnacle, and then there are those whose lasting glory evolves into a dynasty.

Paris St-Germain begin their Champions League campaign on Wednesday hoping to enter that bracket, attempting to become continental champions for a third successive season.

To mark this, we're looking at how the Parisians compare to those clubs who have enjoyed the most dominant eras in European competition.

Some will point out that football existed before the European Champion Clubs' Cup began in 1955 - so apologies to Stan Cullis' 'world-champion' Wolves outfit and the Mitropa Cup's early Vienna heavyweights.

However, this top 10 debate is centred around winning European football's grandest prize.

OK, straight in with the current champions, because this is a dynasty in the making.

PSG have had a lacklustre start to the season - they always do this, don't they? However, you wouldn't bet against Luis Enrique's slick side adding a third successive European crown come next summer.

The Parisians have been France's most dominant force since the arrival of Qatar Sports Investments 15 years ago, but it took a change of approach for the holy grail of continental success to arrive.

"It's the end of the glitter," professed president Nasser Al-Khelaifi after years of lavish spending, ushering out the "flashy, bling-bling" era.

Instead, Enrique arrived in 2023 intent on building a coherent team. There was still significant investment, but on younger players who could be moulded by his philosophy and discipline while given room to flourish.

The result was two scintillating Champions League triumphs.

Talking of discipline. Helenio Herrera, the Argentine-born defender reared in Casablanca and Paris, had already traversed the dugouts of Atletico Madrid, Malaga, Deportivo and Barcelona before landing in Milan in 1960.

Herrera set about implementing his tactical brand of catenaccio at San Siro - one he insisted is misremembered as being more defensive than it actually was - and developing a ruthless counter-attacking team known as 'Grande Inter'.

Winning the Scudetto in 1962-63, Herrera's outfit became the first to lift the European Cup without losing a game the following season as Sandro Mazzola netted twice against Real Madrid in the final.

The Italians defended their crown the following year, despite losing their semi-final first leg at Anfield, edging Benfica in the final. It was the Portuguese giants' second final defeat in three seasons. Some may say they were cursed...

The story goes that Bela Guttmann, fresh from winning the title with Porto, rocked up at Benfica, sacked all the senior players and promoted a talented bunch of youth team players instead.

Those promising youngsters won the title and then went all the way in the European Cup, beating Barcelona in the 1961 final.

That summer, a teenage Eusebio also joined Guttmann's squad and steered them to European glory once more, seeing off Tottenham Hotspur in the semi-final before beating the great Real Madrid in the competition's showpiece.

The legendary Ferenc Puskas scored a first-half hat-trick for the Spaniards, but Eusebio netted twice after the interval to seal Benfica a second successive crown.

Guttmann, buoyed by his remarkable success, left the club after not being offered the pay rise he felt he deserved and the curse the Hungarian boss supposedly put on the club - that they would not win another European trophy for 100 years - has become fable.

Whether the often-disputed story is true or not, the Lisbon giants have not landed another since - losing eight European finals, including three in the 1960s.

This was Bayern's coming of age. Emerging from what was a fiercely competitive West German football scene, the Bavarians - promoted to the Bundesliga less than a decade earlier - were able to establish themselves as heavyweights in Europe.

With a backbone of goalkeeper Sepp Maier, marauding sweeper Franz Beckenbauer and the prolific Gerd Muller, and fresh off West Germany winning the 1974 World Cup, Bayern clinched three on the bounce, despite their domestic form dipping.

In fact, Beckenbauer said Bayern were past their peak after the first European Cup win over Atletico Madrid, but experience carried them through big games.

They beat Leeds in a controversial final in Paris, and then saw off Saint-Etienne the following year.

The teams above make the list for their trophy-winning spells. Pep Guardiola's Barcelona were European champions twice in three years - losing to Jose Mourinho's treble-winning Inter in between - but their dynasty was built on more than silverware.

Guardiola only spent four seasons at Barcelona, but it was an era-defining tenure, the Catalan giants pioneering a brand of football that would be celebrated and copied the world over.

Perhaps the real success of a team is in its legacy. Guardiola's tiki-taka Barcelona built around La Masia graduates Xavi, Andres Iniesta, Sergio Busquets and, of course, Lionel Messi still resonates more than a decade since he left.

Where does this particular Milan dynasty start and end? It was fuelled, of course, by Silvio Berlusconi, who saved the club from bankruptcy in 1986 and appointed the up-and-coming Arrigo Sacchi as boss.

You could argue it continued until a Champions League final defeat by a young Ajax side in 1995. In between, the Rossoneri won back-to-back European Cups in 1989 and '90, then thrashed Cruyff's Barcelona 'Dream Team' in 1994 after defeat in the final the previous season.

In fact, the only campaigns in which Milan did not reach the final were after their quarter-final second leg was abandoned because of floodlight failure while trailing Marseille in 1991. The Serie A giants' refusal to re-enter the pitch for the final minutes of that one also led to them being banned the following year.

From Sacchi to Fabio Capello, through the brilliant Dutch trio of Ruud Gullit, Marco van Basten and Frank Rijkaard to homegrown stars Franco Baresi, Paolo Maldini and Alessandro Costacurta - the Italian core remaining from that 1989 triumph to the defeat by Ajax six years later - Milan were a phenomenal force.

In an era of English dominance on the continent, winning seven of eight European Cups between 1977 and 1984, Liverpool's 'Boot Room' boys led the way.

The Reds won four of those, Nottingham Forest - who could argue they also deserve a spot on the list - went back-to-back and Aston Villa completed the haul.

Liverpool's European pedigree really began when Bill Shankly's side won the Uefa Cup in 1973, the Reds doing it again three years later under Shankly's former assistant Bob Paisley.

Paisley was able to deliver the biggest prize of all the following season in Rome and, after Kenny Dalglish was brought in to replace Hamburg-bound Kevin Keegan, retained the European Cup at Wembley against Club Brugge in 1978 - the Scottish forward netting the winner.

Three years later, after Brian Clough took Forest to the top, Liverpool were European champions again when Alan Kennedy's goal downed Real Madrid in Paris.

Perhaps most impressive is how the Anfield outfit were able to maintain that success through a series of managers. The line of succession from Shankly to Paisley then landed on Joe Fagan, who was in charge when they beat Roma - in Rome - in '84. That was before the Heysel disaster, and defeat by Juventus, the following year.

Atletico fans look away now. Two finals in three years and twice Diego Simeone's side ran into their Madrid rivals, losing in agonising fashion in both 2014 and 2016.

The second of those also sparked a three-year winning run for the most successful club in European Cup history.

Real Madrid's formula was seemingly simple: construct a team of the world's best players - spearheaded by Cristiano Ronaldo - and stick a legendary former star in charge.

Zinedine Zidane's new-era galacticos just felt inevitable - they always found a way to win, becoming the first club in the Champions League era not only to retain the trophy but to lift three in a row.

After downing Atletico in the first of the three-peat, they beat Juventus and then Liverpool - the latter remembered for Gareth Bale's cameo, Loris Karius' blunders and Sergio Ramos leaving his mark on Mo Salah.

Similar to Guardiola's Barcelona, the influence of this Ajax side was seen far beyond the trophy cabinet. The lineage of their philosophy - via Johan Cruyff - survives through several of the clubs on this list, from Catalonia to Paris.

Rinus Michels was the pioneer, taking Ajax from the threat of relegation to the most dominant side in Europe, losing the 1969 final to AC Milan but returning to win it for the first time two years later with their swaggering brand of Total Football.

Michels left for Barcelona on the back of that success, though Stefan Kovacs was able to retain the trophy the following year and then add a third successive European crown to Ajax's pile with an impressive run that included knocking out Bayern Munich, Real Madrid and then Juventus in the final.

Cruyff, about to win the second of his three Ballon d'Ors, followed Michels to Barcelona and Ajax's dynasty began to fall apart. The legacy, however, remains.

When it comes to dominance, no one compares to the Real Madrid side who stormed to five successive European Cup triumphs after the competition began in 1955.

With the tournament in its infancy, it was perhaps not considered as imperative by certain nations compared to how Champions League participation dominates clubs' thoughts today, but Real Madrid's style and success helped to alter perceptions.

Alfredo Di Stefano, already a world star by the time Real beat Reims in the inaugural final, was an integral part of the Spanish giants' success, the legendary Paco Gento likewise a stalwart (he also won a sixth European Cup in 1966).

Then, in 1958, Madrid added Hungarian genius Ferenc Puskas following his two-year ban for refusing to return to Budapest after the revolution in 1956.

Puskas was 31 when he joined, but scored 35 goals in 39 European Cup games for Real Madrid, including four in the 7-3 win over Frankfurt at Hampden in the 1960 final. Di Stefano grabbed the other three as Madrid made it five on the spin.

title: Which NFL team should you support?
description: As the NFL returns for a new season, BBC Sport helps you choose your ideal team to follow.
fullText:
Some 213 days after the Seattle Seahawks beat the New England Patriots at Super Bowl 60, the NFL returns, with the same sides meeting again to open the season.

On Wednesday (01:20 BST, Thursday) the Patriots travel to Lumen Field to play a Seahawks team hoping to become only the ninth franchise to win the title in consecutive seasons.

If you're in the market for a team to follow this year, BBC Sport is here to help.

We've crunched the numbers on a wide range of categories to put the information at your fingertips - and there's a handy quiz at the end to help you figure out your best fit.

Let's start with the top dogs - the trophy winners.

Leading the way with six Super Bowls each are the Pittsburgh Steelers and the Patriots, the latter all coming since the turn of the century under legendary coach Bill Belichick.

Not far behind are the Dallas Cowboys, known as 'America's team', and the San Francisco 49ers, who have each won five.

Taking in the pre-Super Bowl era, the Green Bay Packers have the most NFL championships with 13, including four Super Bowl wins.

At the other end of the spectrum, 12 franchises have never won the Vince Lombardi Trophy, including the Buffalo Bills and the Minnesota Vikings, who have both lost four times in the Super Bowl.

Perhaps silverware isn't everything to you.

If history is more your bag, four teams have been around for 100 years or more. The Arizona Cardinals, Chicago Bears, New York Giants and Green Bay Packers were all established in the 1920s.

For those who prefer more modern upstarts, look no further than the Houston Texans, who only started competing in the NFL in 2002.

We took a calculation of the centre of the UK being a location in Lancashire and figured out the distance from that point to each franchise's stadium in the US.

East Coast teams such as the New England Patriots, Philadelphia Eagles and the two New York teams - the Giants and Jets - are the closest by that metric, coming in at just over 3,000 miles away.

If you would prefer to get as far away from home as possible, shoot across the US towards the Pacific Ocean and opt for the Los Angeles Chargers or Rams, fully 5,263 miles away as the crow flies.

Any NFL game is a major event and, as amply demonstrated during the football World Cup this summer, the US is full of stadiums to suit.

We took the average attendance for each team over the past five seasons to calculate the biggest - and it was the AT&T Stadium in Dallas, where England played their opening group game against Croatia.

The lowest average was the Chicago Bears, with element-exposed Soldier Field the only stadium to come in under 60,000.

The franchise are developing plans for a venue across the state border in Hammond, Indiana.

Taking US weather data from 1991 to 2020, we looked at the range of temperatures from highest to lowest across all 32 areas.

It is no surprise that the hottest areas will affect desert teams Arizona Cardinals and Las Vegas Raiders, with Florida's Miami Dolphins and Tampa Bay Buccaneers also offering scorching summers and mild winters.

If that is not for you, then 12 franchises have an average lowest temperature under freezing, including the Vikings, whose average in January is -8C.

Since first jetting to London in 2013, the Jacksonville Jaguars have played in the UK 14 times, and will stretch that further when they play back-to-back weeks there in October.

That number far outstrips every other franchise, with the Buffalo Bills playing six times in the now defunct Toronto Series of the mid-2000s and twice in London, and the Miami Dolphins third with seven overseas games.

The NFL continues to extend its reach with nine international games planned for 2026, including a maiden trip to Australia when the San Francisco 49ers face the LA Rams at the Melbourne Cricket Ground on opening weekend.

The Dallas Cowboys, whose only previous appearance on foreign soil was in 2014 at Wembley against the Jaguars, will play the Baltimore Ravens at another iconic world stadium, the Maracana in Rio de Janeiro, at the end of September.
