title: LIV files for bankruptcy protection with over $45m owed to players
description: LIV Golf has filed for bankruptcy protection with at least $45m (£33m) owed to players, who will now have the option to leave.
fullText:
LIV Golf has filed for bankruptcy protection with at least $45m (£33m) owed to players, who will now have the option to leave.

A Chapter 11 petition, which LIV says is to "preserve the company's business" as it attempts to restructure after Saudi Arabia withdrew its multibillion-dollar funding, was filed in the United States on Tuesday.

The breakaway league says it has found a new investor in BC Partners, following the decision in April by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund (PIF) to pull its funding.

Documents in the petition outline money owed to LIV Golf's creditors with the 30 largest unsecured claims. Two-time major winner Jon Rahm tops that list with an unsecured claim of $7.5m (£5.5m).

Bryson DeChambeau ($5.7m - £4.2m), Dustin Johnson ($5.5m - £4.1m), Cameron Smith ($4.8m - £3.5m) and Tyrrell Hatton ($3.4m - £2.5m) are also among the top 30 creditors, as well as Brooks Koepka, who left to rejoin the PGA Tour in January but has an unsecured claim of $1.7m (£1.25m).

The total amount owed to the 14 current and former LIV players in the top 30 creditors is just over $45m (£33m).

A source familiar with the figures told BBC Sport the creditors list outlines the "amount owed and not paid for Q3" of 2026, not the full amounts.

The court documents show LIV estimates its assets at $100m-$500m (£74m-£370m) and its liabilities at between $500m and $1bn (£370m-£739m).

LIV Golf intends to commence its new majority player-owned league early next year and it is understood the Chapter 11 process allows it to start talking to players about their participation in LIV's future.

BBC Sport understands there is no obligation on players to sign on to LIV 2.0, regardless of whether they had previously signed multi-year contracts with LIV Golf.

Sources have said contracts under the previous iteration of LIV Golf will finish because of this court filing, with amounts owed to players and other creditors addressed through the court process.

However, it remains unclear when players would then be able to enter discussions with other tours.

'Time will tell' - Rahm on LIV Golf future

Strained smiles and uncertainty - the strange end of LIV Golf 1.0

Saudi Arabia to stop funding LIV Golf next season

Since LIV's controversial launch in 2021, more than $5bn (£3.7bn) has been spent by PIF, with major winners including Rahm and DeChambeau lured by lucrative contracts and vast prize money.

However, the future of the concept - and its star players - has been shrouded in uncertainty, with the 2026 season having ended early.

LIV Golf chief executive Scott O'Neil told the BBC at the final event in Indianapolis last month he had "high levels of confidence" in achieving a "critical mass" of players to make the new league a reality.

DeChambeau said at the conclusion of that event he felt there was "a lot of potential moving forward" and he believed there was "something fun coming".

Speaking on Tuesday before this week's Irish Open, Rahm was tight-lipped when pressed on his future.

Asked if he knew what the coming months held, he told BBC Sport: "Yes and no. It hasn't really changed from my last interview in Indianapolis.

"There's just a lot of things in place, right? There's a lot of things that could happen and it's one of those things where time's gonna tell."

Rahm added: "I still have a contract with LIV 1.0 that I'm more than willing to fulfil, so like I said, time will tell."

The bankruptcy filing was made in the federal district court of New Jersey, where LIV Golf set up a subsidiary earlier in the summer.

Chapter 11 protection postpones a US company's obligations to its creditors, giving it time to reorganise its debts or sell parts of the business.

PIF is providing a bankruptcy loan of $49.6m (£36.6m) - called 'debtor in possession' (DIP) financing - to help fund the process.

When announcing its decision to withdraw funding, PIF said the "substantial investment required by LIV Golf over a longer term" was "no longer consistent" with its strategy.

Despite its decision to stop bankrolling LIV Golf, PIF added it "remains committed" to its "substantial current and future investments in various sports as a priority sector".

On Tuesday, LIV confirmed international investment firm BC Partners as its proposed new investor in a letter to fans outlining its "next phase".

"LIV Golf has entered a court-supervised restructuring process that provides us with the time and framework to address previous financial obligations and complete a transaction that will make the league's next phase a reality," said the letter.

"Put simply, this process is designed to build a stronger and more sustainable future for LIV Golf."

O'Neil added in a statement: "This process gives us the structure and time to pursue a landmark transaction and begin the next chapter of LIV Golf - one built around the fans, an innovative, player-first ownership model, and a part of the global golf ecosystem."

In yet another indication the free-spending days of LIV 1.0 are over, the letter said the new league would be "built around a sustainable business model".

Players are set to be given equity and individual commercial rights are set to be returned to players, giving them greater earning potential. In terms of prize money, LIV Golf purses are set to be lower than events on the PGA Tour - which has risen in part because of the existence of LIV - but higher than events on the DP World Tour.

The letter also outlined proposed changes, with field sizes expanding to 75 players, the introduction of a cut, creating qualifiers and having more teams that "embrace national identities", with the ambitions for teams to "grow into enduring global sports businesses".

LIV cancels final event to focus on 'next chapter'

Is Saudi Arabia's sports revolution unravelling?

What now for Rahm, DeChambeau and LIV's biggest names?

title: Bouaddi impresses on first start - have Man City found 'a gem'?
description: Ayyoub Bouaddi belies his age with a mature Champions League performance on his first Manchester City start to showcase why the club were so intent on signing the 18-year-old.
fullText:
Ayyoub Bouaddi belied his age with a mature Champions League performance on his first Manchester City start to showcase why the club were so intent on signing the 18-year-old.

The midfielder took centre stage for Morocco at this summer's World Cup and City spent £86m to sign him from Lille, making him the most expensive teenager in Premier League history.

And after two substitute appearances for City, he was handed his first start against Porto and did not look out of place during the 2-0 victory.

Erling Haaland will take the plaudits for his two goals, but it was Bouaddi who caught the eye with a tidy and assured performance in the middle of the park, signalling early signs that Rodri may not be too sorely missed after his departure.

"His age, his game – he looks absolutely born to do it," former Chelsea winger Pat Nevin said on BBC Radio 5 Live during the game.

"I cannot take my eyes off Bouaddi, he looks very special. The City fans had the fear of losing Rodri - I watched Bouaddi playing against Scotland at the World Cup, he has been very impressive so far.

"Bouaddi is an absolute no-brainer. He is brilliant. You get him at that age and you don't think he might work, he is a class act."

Haaland nets double as Man City begin Champions League with win at Porto

Aged 18 years and 341 days, Ayyoub Bouaddi became the fourth-youngest player to start a Champions League match for City.

Question marks were raised around the size of the fee for a position on the pitch where players can be exposed, but Bouaddi seems to have settled in immediately and showcased why he will be a valuable option this season.

"He is very good," said manager Enzo Maresca. "Against Coventry, he lost two balls and after that he was inside our box and calm. Other players may have panicked but at 18, he is a fantastic player.

"Tonight, he was very good. He speaks French, English, Spanish perfect. He is different in how mature he is. This is why the club has made the effort for him to be with us."

BBC Sport reported City's interest in Bouaddi in June and, contrary to reports, sources said signing him and then loaning back to Lille for a season was not on the agenda.

The performance in Portugal highlighted why those in power at City believe he has all attributes to "develop into a world class talent" and he clearly enjoys playing on the biggest stage.

Two years ago, Bouaddi earned a standing ovation from Lille supporters after helping his side to a shock group phase victory over holders Real Madrid and the travelling City fans will have been doing the same in Portugal on Tuesday evening.

Bouaddi completed 54 of his 55 passes, while he also topped the metrics across players of both sides for most dribbles (4), most times possession won (7) and contesting more duels (13).

"He did a really good game," said Haaland. "The last couple of weeks in training, he has been amazing. I think we have got a gem there, to be honest."

Though it was only Bouaddi's 10th appearance in the competition, the Norwegian sent a playful yet pointed message to his team-mate about needing to be perfect all of the time.

The striker added: "I think he should've played me through in the second half so I was a bit angry.

"But he played a good game... except for that pass."

title: Tiafoe consoles tearful Michelsen after remarkable US Open comeback
description: Frances Tiafoe comes from two sets and a break down to beat Alex Michelsen in a thrilling comeback to reach the US Open semi-finals.
fullText:
Frances Tiafoe came from two sets and a break down to beat fellow American Alex Michelsen in a thrilling comeback to reach the US Open semi-finals.

Eleventh seed Tiafoe was outplayed by world number 46 Michelsen for the first half of the match, but battled back from 5-3 down in the third set - with his opponent serving for the match - to ignite a remarkable turnaround.

In a final set of multiple breaks and swings of momentum, Tiafoe triumphed in the 10-point tie-break to win 5-7 3-6 7-5 6-3 7-6 (10-6).

Victory means 28-year-old Tiafoe reaches his third US Open semi-final in five years, where he will play defending champion Carlos Alcaraz or American eighth seed Ben Shelton.

Michelsen, 22, who was competing in his first Grand Slam quarter-final, was in tears as the pair embraced after a match which lasted four hours and 38 minutes.

"In the end I slowly started to get my rhythm. Snuck out that third set and got better and better," said Tiafoe.

"He's a hell of a player and he easily could have won today. Shout out to Alex Michelsen.

"Everyone was asleep in the first couple of hours, I was too. As it went along the energy was incredible as it is always. You guys are rooting for me and I appreciate that."

Sabalenka fights back to keep US Open defence alive

Hewett and Reid bid for sixth US Open title

Sabalenka beats Noskova in epic & do we need 5 sets?

Unseeded Michelsen came into the match in fine form, having not dropped a set at the tournament prior to facing Tiafoe, and grasped the momentum in the first set.

After the pair traded breaks of serve early in the match, Michelsen got the deciding break at 6-5 in a set where he fired 15 winners to Tiafoe's four.

Michelsen continued to have the upper hand, with his backhand proving decisive on key points and, after taking the second set, he went up a break early in the third.

It was not until Michelsen was serving for the match at 5-4 that nerves began to hit. He served two double faults and Tiafoe broke to level, won the set and took the opening three games of the fourth set.

After holding Michelsen off, Tiafoe took the match to a deciding set where the pair traded multiple breaks of serve - invigorating the spectators on Arthur Ashe Stadium.

A fan favourite, Tiafoe thrived off the energy of the New York crowd as he then got the better of the tie-break to seal his fourth five-set victory at a major in 2026.

Tiafoe is hoping to reach the final at Flushing Meadows for the first time, following defeats by Alcaraz in 2022 and Taylor Fritz in 2024.

title: West Ham go top of Championship - are they ready to leave past behind?
description: Three wins in a row, top of the table, unity at the club - are West Ham ready to leave the past behind on and off the pitch?
fullText:
It was a night to remember for West Ham and their 4,500-travelling support.

Skipper and club talisman Jarrod Bowen opened the scoring early, then secured victory late in a five-goal thriller at Bolton.

The result took West Ham to the top of the Championship. It was their third successive league win - the first time they have done that since December 2023.

That was the run which prompted a contract offer to David Moyes that went unsigned and was eventually withdrawn prior to the Scot's departure six months later. The decline continued and ended in relegation last May.

With elation in short supply recently, West Ham's fans made sure they enjoyed this night, staying to acknowledge their team after the final whistle, delaying departure on a journey that, for many, won't end until the middle of the night.

Amid homage to Bowen, singing about bubbles and West Ham being 'massive', the visiting supporters also chanted repeatedly about former chairman David Sullivan. None of the songs about him were complimentary.

Bowen double helps West Ham beat Bolton to go top

Sullivan was not at Bolton for the Championship encounter. He has been at all of the Hammers' home games so far this season, though. He was also at Watford for a 1-1 draw last month.

For some, this involvement is a surprise.

When the 77-year-old resigned as chairman in June, saying his intention was to fight allegations made against him in a joint BBC Panorama and Times investigation, there was an expectation it would eventually trigger his exit from the club.

That and Karren Brady standing down as managing director in April, had been cited as a significant factor in West Ham selling a remarkable 50,000 season tickets for their first campaign outside the top flight since 2011.

Their average home crowd in the league so far tops 60,000. The 53,369 who watched their EFL Cup first round victory over Portsmouth was a record for that stage of the competition.

But Sullivan remains. Providing the complicated agreement announced on 3 September goes through as anticipated within the next few weeks, he will end up with 40% of the club. Sullivan has clearly not disappeared from the West Ham picture.

He is nowhere near as influential, though.

Talk to people inside the club and they will tell you how much has changed since the summer.

Czech billionaire and Royal Mail owner Daniel Kretinsky is now chairman. It is intended he will become the biggest shareholder with 46%.

Karim Virani is making a positive impression as chief executive. He has earned praise for his willingness to engage with supporters and confront issues important to them, not least the club's badge, which was changed in 2016 to coincide with the move away from the Boleyn Ground.

Director of football Nils Koppen has influence in recruitment discussions. Recruitment as a whole is now a transparent affair involving the right people within the club rather than deals being executed without adequate discussion.

In a summer of huge change, 12 players were sold - including Crysencio Summerville and Mateus Fernandes - and, eventually, nine came in.

West Ham paid an EFL record £22m to Celtic for Belgium international Arne Engels. But it is the arrival of Edvin Austbo, the 21-year-old named Norway's young player of the year for his role in the Viking's shock Eliteserien title triumph, that they view as evidence of change. Austbo had been tracked for a decent period of time before West Ham executed the transfer, for an initial £10m.

Yet, this being West Ham, the situation is not quite so straightforward.

Uncertainty remains over the intentions of Amanda Staveley. It was the former Newcastle director's deal with former co-chair Vanessa Gold in July that triggered the pre-emption rights process at West Ham which eventually led to the deal that not only sees Kretinsky and Sullivan increase their stakes, but also fellow shareholders Tripp Smith and Terry Brown.

In theory, if Staveley agreed a deal with Sullivan and Smith, who will have 11%, she would own over half the club.

Yet that would also be subject to pre-emption rights.

Sullivan talks positively about Kretinsky privately and is unhappy the recent process diverted attention away from the transfer window. His words do not seem to be those of someone about to create even more turmoil at the London Stadium.

"It seemed Sullivan was going when he stepped down, but that hasn't happened," said Simon Lane, a Hammers season ticket holder from north Wales, who stopped for a chat 90 minutes before kick-off.

"No-one really knows what to make of it all. Does he want more shares? Does he want to get out? Why would he do a deal with Kretinsky and then sell the whole thing?

"It's difficult to know what is for the best really. Some fans do like what Amanda Staveley did at Newcastle but Kretinsky puts the right people in place and Karim is talking with fans, which is what we have wanted.

"I am optimistic for the season though."

In Bowen, Engels and others, West Ham have class few Championship rivals can match.

Nuno knows a successful club needs more than that.

Stability and unity are not words often used about West Ham in recent years. But Nuno can see the path to a bright future.

"I hope it's better," he said. "I think it's the belief of everybody, starting from the ownership to the staff, to the players, and fans, that we are trying to improve and have better days.

"What I see, and feel is unity in all the departments of the club. Five thousand fans on a Tuesday night. (What happened in the past) is behind us. It's very important to be unified. There is no other way."
